title: Alignment Tax in Practice
description: Measuring the real cost of safety measures
body_head: # Alignment Tax in Practice  ## Summary Alignment tax in practice measures the capability delta between safe and unsafe versions of the same system.  ## Details - Alignment tax in practice measures the capability delta between safe and unsafe versions of the same system. - Honest measurement requires identical evals, controlling for training randomness. - Small measured taxes make safety cheap; large taxes change competitive dynamics. - RSIS3 relevance: practice-check overhead is the bundle's measured tax.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/alignment-tax|Alignment Tax]] — the concept - [[wiki/concepts/capability-vs-alignment|Capability vs Alignment]] — the axes - [[wiki/concepts/safety-evals-pr

title: Alignment Tax
description: The performance cost of making an AI system safe rather than just capable
body_head: # Alignment Tax  ## Summary The alignment tax is the capability cost paid for alignment: guardrails, filters, and training constraints that trade raw benchmark performance for safety. Whether the tax is small or large determines whether aligned systems can compete with unaligned ones — a central question for competitive pressure models.  ## Details - **Forms** — safety training reduces some benchmark scores; sandboxing slows agents; oversight consumes compute. - **Evidence** — RLHF and Constitutional AI show modest taxes on many tasks, sometimes near zero, sometimes large for specialized skills. - **Strategic role** — if the tax is large, competitive markets reward skipping safety; if smal

title: Ambiguity Aversion
description: Preferring known risks over unknown probabilities
body_head: # Ambiguity Aversion  ## Summary  Ambiguity aversion is the tendency to prefer options with known probabilities over options whose probabilities are unknown, even when expected values are equal. It matters because it shapes real choices — insurance, investment, and novel technology adoption — and explains behaviors that expected-utility theory cannot. The classic demonstration is the Ellsberg paradox.  ## Details  - **Definition** — Given two gambles with identical expected value, people systematically avoid the one with unspecified probabilities, revealing a distaste for ambiguity itself. - **Ellsberg paradox** — Urns with known versus unknown color compositions elicit preferences that vi

title: Analogical Reasoning
description: Transferring structure from a known situation to a new one
body_head: # Analogical Reasoning  ## Summary Analogical reasoning maps structure from a source situation to a target, transferring solutions or predictions. It matters because analogy is how agents apply past experience to novel but structurally similar problems. It underlies case-based reasoning and few-shot learning.  ## Details - Requires identifying relational structure, not surface similarity. - Strong analogy = deep structural alignment. - In LLMs: analogy is implicit in few-shot prompting. - Open questions: evaluating the soundness of model analogies.  ## Related - [[wiki/llm-agents/self-reflection-agents|Self-Reflection Agents]] — analogy in self-review - [[wiki/concepts/case-based-reasoning

title: Analogical Transfer
description: Applying knowledge from one situation to another via analogy
body_head: # Analogical Transfer  ## Summary  Analogical Transfer — Applying knowledge from one situation to another via analogy. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Transfer succeeds when relational structure matches, even if surfaces differ. - Gick & Holyoak: spontaneous transfer is rare unless the analogy is pointed out. - Abstraction and multiple examples boost transfer. - Core mechanism of learning by example and case-based reasoning.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/structure-mapping-theory|Structure Mapping Theory]] — mapping account - [[wiki/concepts/surface-similarity|Surface Similarity]] — blocker - [[wiki/memory/trans

title: Answer Set Programming
description: Declarative problem solving via stable-model semantics
body_head: # Answer Set Programming  ## Summary Answer set programming (ASP) is a declarative programming paradigm for solving hard combinatorial search problems. You write a description of what a valid solution looks like — rules and constraints — and an ASP solver computes the answer sets, which are the stable models satisfying the program. The programmer specifies the problem, not the algorithm.  ## Details - A program consists of facts, rules, and constraints. A rule has the form `head :- body`, meaning the head holds when the body holds; constraints are rules with an empty head that forbid certain combinations; and choice rules let the solver decide a range of truth values. title: Arbitration
description: Binding resolution of disputes that discussion cannot settle
body_head: # Arbitration  ## Summary Arbitration is the binding dispute-resolution step for conflicts that discussion, mediation, and consensus have failed to settle.  ## Details - An arbitration body hears the case, applies policy, and issues a decision that is binding and recorded. - Arbitration is expensive and slow, which is exactly why it is the last resort — its cost pushes earlier steps to work. - For mykb, arbitration handles policy-breaking conduct and intractable content disputes, and its decisions become precedent.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/arbitration|Arbitration]] - [[wiki/concepts/mediation-wiki|Mediation]] - [[wiki/concepts/dispute-resolution-wiki|Dispute Resolution]] - [[wiki/conc

title: Archival Criteria
description: When an article moves out of the active wiki into the archive
body_head: # Archival Criteria  ## Summary Archival criteria define the transition from active wiki content to preserved-but-inactive storage: topic superseded, permanently stale, or merged into a broader article.  ## Details - Archival preserves the record — the file moves rather than disappears, keeping provenance and history for future reference. - The criteria should be conservative: archiving is cheaper to delay than to undo, because readers lose the article's discoverability immediately. - For mykb, archival criteria pair with deletion criteria: archive when the content still has reference value, delete only when it never did.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/deletion-criteria|Deletion Criteria]]

title: Arousal and Performance
description: Relationship between physiological activation and task performance
body_head: # Arousal and Performance  ## Summary  Arousal and performance describes how physiological activation — alertness, energy, stress — relates to task performance, famously summarized as an inverted-U function. Moderate arousal supports optimal performance while very low or very high activation degrades it. The relationship matters for designing stakes, schedules, and environments that keep performers in the productive range.  ## Details  - **Definition** — Arousal is the level of physiological and psychological activation; performance measures task success as a function of that level. - **Inverted U** — Performance improves with arousal up to an optimum and declines beyond it; the optimum sh

title: Article Quality Checklist
description: Review criteria for promoting mykb articles from stub to full
body_head: # Article Quality Checklist  ## Summary The article quality checklist is the review criteria mykb uses to decide when an article is good enough to leave stub status. It turns "this article should be better" from a taste judgment into a checkable list: substance, structure, links, provenance, and RSIS3 relevance.  ## Details - Substance is the first gate. A stub is a definition; a full article explains mechanisms, gives concrete examples, and names failure modes and tradeoffs. The checklist asks: could a reader reproduce or apply the idea from this page alone? If the answer is no, the article still needs work regardless of word count, because length without specificity is padding. - Structu

title: Atomic Articles
description: Articles covering exactly one idea
body_head: # Atomic Articles  ## Summary Atomic articles cover exactly one idea, following the evergreen-note principle that each concept deserves its own addressable page.  ## Details - Atomicity makes links precise: a reader linking to a page knows what they are linking to, and the graph stays clean. - Atomicity is enforced by split-criteria and merge-criteria — pages that violate it get restructured, not tolerated. - For mykb, atomic articles are the norm, and compound articles are the deliberate exception.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/compound-articles|Compound Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/atomic-articles|Atomic Articles]] - [[wiki/wiki/memory/evergreen-note-taking|Evergreen Note-Taking]] - [[wi

description: Selection processes that decide what information an agent focuses on
body_head: # Attention Mechanisms  ## Summary Attention mechanisms allocate processing and context to the most relevant information, whether in the model's internal computation or the agent's retrieval choices. They matter because selection determines what the agent actually considers. Attention is what keeps context manageable.  ## Details - Internal: transformer attention weights select relevant tokens. - External: agent-level attention chooses which files, memories, and tools to consult. - RSIS3 relevance: retrieval selection and prompt construction are attention policies. - Open questions: aligning agent-level attention with task relevance. - Attention mechanisms in machine learning let a model s

description: Missed second target when it appears ~200-500ms after the first in rapid streams
body_head: # Attentional Blink  ## Summary  Attentional Blink — Missed second target when it appears ~200-500ms after the first in rapid streams. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - In rapid serial visual presentation, the second of two targets is often missed. - Reflects a capacity bottleneck in temporal attention. - Blink size varies with target similarity and training. - Evidence for limited attentional resources over time.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/selective-attention|Selective Attention]] — resource limits - [[wiki/concepts/sustained-attention|Sustained Attention]] — temporal dimension - [[wiki/memory/attention-and-c

title: Authority Weighting
description: Giving well-established articles more weight
body_head: # Authority Weighting  ## Summary Authority weighting gives articles that are established — verified, reviewed, stable — more weight than new or unverified ones.  ## Details - It encodes the sensible bias that proven content should outrank unproven content. - Authority must be earned through the review pipeline, or the weight simply rewards age. - For mykb, authority weighting is built from verification history and reviewed status, and it feeds search ranking.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/weight-articles|Weighting Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/authority-weighting|Authority Weighting]] - [[wiki/concepts/verified-tag|Verified Tag]] - [[wiki/concepts/stable-articles|Stable Articles]] - [[wiki

title: Autoconfirmed
description: Editor status earned automatically after sufficient activity
body_head: # Autoconfirmed  ## Summary Autoconfirmed is editor status earned automatically once an account passes an age-and-edit threshold, unlocking higher-trust actions.  ## Details - Automation removes judgment from the gate: the threshold is fixed, objective, and reviewed periodically. - Autoconfirmation is a floor, not a badge — it filters casual noise, not sophisticated bad actors. - For mykb, autoconfirmed status gates semi-protected pages and is recorded in contribution history.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/autoconfirmed|Autoconfirmed]] - [[wiki/concepts/registered-editors|Registered Editors]] - [[wiki/concepts/semi-protected|Semi-Protected]] - [[wiki/concepts/new-editors|New Editors]] - [[

body_head: # Autonomy Evals  ## Summary Autonomy evals measure an agent's ability to plan and execute multi-step tasks without human help.  ## Details - Autonomy evals measure an agent's ability to plan and execute multi-step tasks without human help. - High autonomy is a capability and a risk multiplier. - Tasks range from research to long-horizon operations. - RSIS3 relevance: the loop's autonomy is deliberately gated by approvals and checks.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/agentic-risk-evals|Agentic Risk Evals]] — the risk framing - [[wiki/concepts/agent-benchmarks|Agent Benchmarks]] — the measurement - [[wiki/agent-systems/approval-based-agents|Approval-Based Agents]] — the design gate - [[wiki/con

title: Autotuning
description: Automatic search for optimal configuration parameters
body_head: # Autotuning  ## Summary Autotuning is the automatic search for configuration parameters — compiler flags, kernel block sizes, hyperparameters — that optimize a performance or quality metric. It turns tuning from an expert activity into a closed-loop search, often using Bayesian optimization or random search.  ## Details - **Scope** — compiler optimization flags, database knobs, ML hyperparameters, and scheduling policies. - **Methods** — grid/random search, Bayesian optimization, bandit algorithms, and learning-based predictors. - **Why it matters for RSI** — a system that tunes itself removes a human bottleneck from the improvement loop. - **Risks** — tuning to a proxy metric (Goodhart),

title: Axiology
description: The study of what is valuable
body_head: # Axiology  ## Summary Axiology is the philosophical study of value: what is good, worth pursuing, or worth preserving.  ## Details - Axiology is the philosophical study of value: what is good, worth pursuing, or worth preserving. - AI value alignment is applied axiology: choosing a value theory to instantiate. - Core debates: value pluralism, intrinsic vs instrumental value, and value incommensurability. - RSIS3 relevance: the wiki's value pages are an axiological map for the bundle.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/value-specification|Value Specification]] — applied axiology - [[wiki/concepts/moral-uncertainty|Moral Uncertainty]] — axiological doubt - [[wiki/concepts/terminal-goals|Terminal

body_head: # Backdoor Attacks on LLMs  ## Summary Backdoor attacks plant triggers in training data that activate attacker-chosen behavior at inference.  ## Details - Backdoor attacks plant triggers in training data that activate attacker-chosen behavior at inference. - Backdoored models behave normally until the trigger fires. - Detection is hard at scale; provenance and differential inspection help. - RSIS3 relevance: poisoned wiki content could trigger bad retrieval outcomes.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/trojan-attacks|Trojan Attacks]] — the weight-level form - [[wiki/concepts/data-poisoning-practice|Data Poisoning in Practice]] — the delivery - [[wiki/concepts/model-tampering|Model Tampering]] —

title: Backward Chaining
description: Reasoning from a goal backward to known facts
body_head: # Backward Chaining  ## Summary Backward chaining starts from a goal and works backward, finding rules that could prove it and recursively proving their premises. It matters because it focuses inference on what is relevant to the goal. It powers Prolog and many explanation-capable expert systems.  ## Details - Goal-driven: only rules relevant to the current goal fire. - Produces explanations: the derivation tree is the why. - Contrast with forward chaining (data-driven). - Open questions: backward chaining over LLM-generated rules.  ## Related - [[wiki/agent-systems/planning-systems|Planning Systems]] — goal-directed reasoning - [[wiki/concepts/goal-regression|Goal Regression]] — the plann

title: Balanced Articles
description: Articles that fairly represent the significant views
body_head: # Balanced Articles  ## Summary Balanced articles represent the significant views on their subject fairly and proportionately, with each position attributed and weighted by its actual standing.  ## Details - Balance is not 50/50 — a fringe view gets a mention and a rebuttal, not equal billing with the mainstream. - Balance is judged by the article's coverage: what is included, what is excluded, and how each is framed. - For mykb, balanced articles are the target state for contested technical topics and are reviewed under NPOV policy.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/balanced-articles|Balanced Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/biased-articles|Biased Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/npov-policy|NPOV Pol

title: Bans
description: Removing an editor's ability to contribute
body_head: # Bans  ## Summary Bans remove an editor's ability to contribute, imposed for conduct that undermines the wiki — persistent vandalism, sockpuppetry, or repeated policy-breaking.  ## Details - A ban is a process outcome with evidence and a defined scope (temporary or permanent, page or site-wide), not a spontaneous act. - Ban enforcement depends on the wiki being able to identify accounts, which is why registration exists. - For mykb, bans follow the warning and dispute-resolution ladder and are logged with their rationale.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/bans|Bans]] - [[wiki/concepts/warnings-wiki|Warnings]] - [[wiki/concepts/arbitration|Arbitration]] - [[wiki/concepts/sockpuppetry|Sockpuppe

title: Basic AI Goals
description: The minimal objectives any competent agent pursues
body_head: # Basic AI Goals  ## Summary Basic AI goals are the near-universal objectives of competent agents: completing tasks, avoiding failure, preserving existence.  ## Details - Basic AI goals are the near-universal objectives of competent agents: completing tasks, avoiding failure, preserving existence. - Some arise from rationality; others from design choices. - Understanding baseline goal structure helps predict behavior before training details are known. - RSIS3 relevance: the loop's baseline goals (task completion, checkpoint safety) are explicitly documented.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/instrumental-goals|Instrumental Goals]] — the convergent subset - [[wiki/concepts/self-preservation-goa

title: Bayesian Brain
description: Hypothesis that the brain represents and updates probabilistic beliefs
body_head: # Bayesian Brain  ## Summary  Bayesian Brain — Hypothesis that the brain represents and updates probabilistic beliefs. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Neural populations encode probability distributions over hypotheses. - Perception and action minimize expected surprise or free energy. - Explains cue combination, illusions, and sensorimotor control. - A bridge between cognitive science and Bayesian reasoning.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/predictive-processing|Predictive Processing]] — mechanism - [[wiki/concepts/bayesian-reasoning|Bayesian Reasoning]] — normative side - [[wiki/concepts/perception-as-inference|

title: Bayesian Networks
description: Graphical models encoding conditional dependencies among variables
body_head: # Bayesian Networks  ## Summary A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) whose nodes are random variables and whose edges encode direct probabilistic dependencies. Each node carries a conditional probability table or distribution over its values given its parents, and the graph's structure lets the joint distribution factor into a product of local terms — the compact representation that makes reasoning tractable.  ## Details - The graph encodes conditional-independence assumptions: a node is independent of its non-descendants given its parents (the Markov condition). That property is both the network's power and its danger. Correct structure shrinks inference dramatically; a mi

title: Bayesian Reasoning
description: Updating beliefs by combining prior probability with new evidence via Bayes' rule
body_head: # Bayesian Reasoning  ## Summary  Bayesian Reasoning — Updating beliefs by combining prior probability with new evidence via Bayes' rule.  ## Details  - Bayesian reasoning applies Bayes' theorem: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. It is the normative standard for belief revision — new evidence reweights hypotheses in proportion to how well they predict the data — and it unifies perception, learning, and decision-making. - Core concepts: priors (initial beliefs), likelihoods (evidence under each hypothesis), posteriors (revised beliefs), and prediction (marginalizing over hypotheses). description: Applying Bayes' rule to revise beliefs with new evidence
body_head: # Bayesian Updating Practice  ## Summary  Bayesian Updating Practice — Applying Bayes' rule to revise beliefs with new evidence. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior; updating is iterative and principled. - Practice: set priors, collect data, compute or approximate posteriors. - Checks: sensitivity to prior, likelihood correctness, and calibration. - Foundation for belief-updating and forecasting systems.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/prior-selection|Prior Selection]] — the prior step - [[wiki/concepts/likelihood-principle|Likelihood Principle]] — evidence step - [[wiki/concepts/poster

title: Belief Bias
description: Accepting conclusions that match prior beliefs regardless of validity
body_head: # Belief Bias  ## Summary  Belief Bias — Accepting conclusions that match prior beliefs regardless of validity. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - People rate believable conclusions as valid even when logic says otherwise. - Strongest with complex or ambiguous arguments. - Reduced but not eliminated by expertise and instruction. - Interacts with dual-process accounts of reasoning.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/syllogistic-reasoning|Syllogistic Reasoning]] — typical paradigm - [[wiki/concepts/dual-process-interventions|Dual Process Interventions]] — countermeasure - [[wiki/memory/schemas-and-stereotypes|Schemas and

title: Belief States
description: The agent's internal model of the world, updated by observations
body_head: # Belief States  ## Summary Belief states are the agent's internal estimate of the world given everything it has seen: what is true, what is uncertain, and what changed. They matter because decisions are only as good as the beliefs they are based on. POMDP theory formalizes beliefs as probability distributions over hidden states.  ## Details - Beliefs update as observations arrive; contradictory evidence should revise them. - Well-calibrated beliefs carry uncertainty, not just point estimates. - Stale beliefs cause confidently wrong actions; agents must re-verify. - Open questions: belief persistence across sessions and belief revision policy. - A belief state is a probability distribution

title: Belief Updating Practice

body_head: # Belief Updating Practice  ## Summary  Belief Updating Practice — Habits and protocols for revising beliefs when evidence arrives. title: Benchmark Contamination

body_head: # Benchmark Contamination  ## Summary Benchmark contamination is the presence of benchmark examples in training data, inflating leaderboard scores.  ## Details - Benchmark contamination is the presence of benchmark examples in training data, inflating leaderboard scores. - LLM-scale web corpora make it near-inevitable for public benchmarks. - Mitigations: hidden benchmarks, contamination audits, and reporting per-sample provenance. - RSIS3 relevance: graph-health metrics are 'contaminated' if the checker and generator share assumptions.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/eval-contamination|Eval Contamination]] — the umbrella - [[wiki/concepts/train-test-contamination|Train-Test Contamination]]

title: Biased Articles
description: Articles whose presentation unfairly favors one side
body_head: # Biased Articles  ## Summary Biased articles present a subject in a way that unfairly favors one side — through selection, framing, or word choice.  ## Details - Bias is often structural: which facts are included and which are omitted is itself a point of view. - Fixing bias requires the article to represent the other sides fairly, not to strip all opinions into mush. - For mykb, biased articles are flagged at review, tagged needs-review, and reworked under the neutral-language conventions.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/biased-articles|Biased Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/balanced-articles|Balanced Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/npov-policy|NPOV Policy]] - [[wiki/concepts/loaded-language|Loa

title: Bidirectional Link Ratio
description: Fraction of links that are reciprocated between pages
body_head: # Bidirectional Link Ratio  ## Summary The bidirectional link ratio measures how many of a wiki's links are reciprocated — if page A links to B, does B link back to A? It is a structural health metric for knowledge graphs: high reciprocity signals a well-connected cluster of mutually relevant notes, while low reciprocity can signal dead ends, hub pages, or one-way dependencies.  ## Details - The metric is computed as the fraction of directed edges that have a reverse edge, either globally (all links in the wiki) or per page (of the pages this article links to, how many link back). title: Bootstrap Problem
description: How an agent validates an improvement using only the competence it already has
body_head: # Bootstrap Problem  ## Summary The bootstrap problem is the catch-22 of recursive self-improvement: to verify that a proposed upgrade is better, you need capabilities you may only get after accepting the upgrade. Every self-improving system must find trustworthy static or external anchors to break the circularity.  ## Details - **Form** — proving P(n+1) better than P(n) looks like it requires P(n+1)'s own judgment. - **Escapes** — hold-out evaluation on frozen benchmarks, external oversight, formal verification of the evaluator, and conservatism about accepting large deltas. - **Relevant failure** — a system that self-rates as improved without external evidence is just flattering itself (

title: Bottom-Up Processing
description: Perception driven by raw sensory features, independent of expectation
body_head: # Bottom-Up Processing  ## Summary  Bottom-Up Processing — Perception driven by raw sensory features, independent of expectation. title: Bounded Rationality
description: Decision-making constrained by limited computation, time, and information
body_head: # Bounded Rationality  ## Summary Bounded rationality describes decision-making under real constraints: limited computation, limited time, and incomplete information. Where classical rational-choice theory assumes an agent that can evaluate all options and pick the optimum, bounded rationality asks what a feasible agent — human or machine — actually does when the optimum is unreachable, and why that behavior can still be remarkably good.  ## Details - Herbert Simon's original formulation distinguished "substantive rationality" (choosing the best option, which requires omniscience) from "procedural rationality" (following a good process under constraints). body_head: # Brier Score  ## Summary  The Brier score measures the accuracy of probabilistic forecasts as the mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and actual outcomes. It matters because it scores calibration and resolution together, rewarding forecasts that are both honest and informative. It is the standard metric for evaluating probability forecasts across weather, medicine, and prediction competitions.  ## Details  - **Definition** — For binary outcomes, the score averages (predicted probability minus outcome) squared; lower is better, with zero for perfect forecasts. - **Decomposition** — The score decomposes into reliability (calibration), resolution (separation of good and b

title: Calibration Curves

body_head: # Calibration Curves  ## Summary  A calibration curve plots predicted probabilities against observed frequencies, showing how well a forecaster's or model's confidence matches reality. It matters because it turns calibration from an abstract property into a visible shape: points on the diagonal mean perfect calibration. Curves expose both overconfidence and underconfidence and guide where recalibration is needed.  ## Details  - **Definition** — Forecasts are binned by predicted probability; each bin's observed event rate is plotted against it, with the diagonal representing perfect calibration. - **Reading the curve** — Points above the diagonal indicate overconfidence (high predictions, l

title: Calibration
description: Agreement between a model's confidence and its accuracy
body_head: # Calibration  ## Summary Calibration is the agreement between a model's stated confidence and its actual accuracy: of all predictions made with 70% confidence, roughly 70% should be correct. A model can be accurate yet badly miscalibrated — highly capable on average while systematically overconfident on the cases that matter — which is why calibration is a core evaluation and safety metric rather than a nicety.  ## Details - The standard measurement is reliability: bin predictions by confidence and compare mean confidence to observed accuracy within each bin. title: Capability Externalities
description: Costs and benefits of AI capability that fall outside the deploying actor
body_head: # Capability Externalities  ## Summary Capability externalities are the third-party effects of AI capability gains — risks and benefits experienced by people who did not choose the deployment. When a lab's capability advances create risks for everyone (or opportunities for bad actors), the market alone will not price them correctly.  ## Details - **Negative externalities** — increased cyber or bio risk, job displacement, and arms-race pressures imposed on others. - **Positive externalities** — cheaper research tools and productivity spillovers. - **Public-goods problem** — safety research is a public good; the market under-provides it, justifying coordination and compute governance. - **Po

title: Capability Forecasting
description: Predicting future AI system capabilities from trends and models
body_head: # Capability Forecasting  ## Summary Capability forecasting estimates how AI capabilities will evolve — from extrapolating scaling curves to expert elicitation and biological anchors. It feeds timelines, compute governance thresholds, and responsible-scaling gates, and it is systematically hard because capability is multidimensional.  ## Details - **Methods** — scaling-law extrapolation (Epoch AI), expert surveys, task-specific benchmarks, and scenario analysis. - **Uncertainty** — frontier capability is fat-tailed; point forecasts routinely miss paradigm shifts. - **Use in safety** — thresholds for dangerous-capability evals and RSP tiers are forecasts operationalized as gates. - **Self-f

title: Capability Jumps
description: Discontinuous increases in model or agent capability
body_head: # Capability Jumps  ## Summary Capability jumps are sudden, large increases in what an AI system can do, whether from a new training paradigm, a self-improvement loop, or a scale threshold. Whether jumps are real or artifacts of measurement drives both takeoff forecasts and the design of capability monitoring.  ## Details - **Sources** — new architectures (transformers), new objectives (RLHF), scaffolding (tool use, test-time compute), and self-improvement. - **Measurement** — many apparent jumps vanish under continuous metrics; genuine jumps show up in raw capability distributions. - **Safety role** — capability monitoring must catch jumps early because misalignment discovered after a jum

title: Capability vs Alignment
description: Separating what a system can do from what it will do
body_head: # Capability vs Alignment  ## Summary Capability is what a system can do; alignment is whether its objectives serve the designer. The two axes are logically independent: a system can be highly capable and misaligned (powerful but pursuing the wrong goal), highly aligned and weak (harmless but useless), or any other combination. Treating them as one measurement is the classic error that produces confident, wrong safety verdicts.  ## Details - A capability measurement answers "can it?" — benchmark scores, dangerous-capability evals, and task success rates. An alignment measurement answers "will it, and for whom?" — goal consistency, constraint compliance, and behavior under stress or adversa

title: Case-Based Reasoning
description: Solving new problems by retrieving and adapting similar past cases
body_head: # Case-Based Reasoning  ## Summary Case-based reasoning (CBR) solves problems by retrieving the most similar past cases from memory and adapting their solutions. It matters because it leverages experience directly instead of abstract rules. Modern RAG agents are CBR with learned retrieval and adaptation.  ## Details - Cycle: retrieve → reuse → revise → retain. - Similarity metrics determine which cases surface. - Retained new cases grow the memory — a learning loop. - Open questions: adaptation quality for open-ended tasks.  ## Related - [[wiki/llm-agents/memory-augmented-agents|Memory-Augmented Agents]] — the memory substrate - [[wiki/concepts/episodic-memory|Episodic Memory]] — the case

title: Catastrophic Misalignment
description: Misalignment with large-scale harmful consequences
body_head: # Catastrophic Misalignment  ## Summary Catastrophic misalignment is misalignment whose consequences are extreme: loss of control, mass harm, or civilization-level damage. It is the outcome where a powerful AI system's goals diverge from human interests on a scale that ordinary safeguards cannot absorb — the difference between a model that occasionally misbehaves and one whose misbehavior compounds into irreversible harm.  ## Details - What makes misalignment catastrophic rather than merely costly is scale and irreversibility. title: Catastrophic Risk
description: Risks of large-scale harm short of extinction
body_head: # Catastrophic Risk  ## Summary Catastrophic risk covers outcomes causing massive harm while civilization survives: pandemics, wars, systemic collapse.  ## Details - Catastrophic risk covers outcomes causing massive harm while civilization survives: pandemics, wars, systemic collapse. - AI contributes both direct risks and amplifiers of existing ones. - Mitigations span technical safety and governance. - RSIS3 relevance: the graph separates catastrophic from existential risk for precision.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/existential-risk|Existential Risk]] — the extreme subset - [[wiki/concepts/global-catastrophic-risk|Global Catastrophic Risk]] — the umbrella - [[wiki/concepts/misalignment-

title: Category Learning
description: How people acquire and refine categories from experience
body_head: # Category Learning  ## Summary  Category learning is the process by which people acquire the ability to group objects, events, or ideas into categories and apply those groupings to new instances. It matters because categories organize perception, memory, and decision-making, and their acquisition follows systematic, testable principles. Theories differ on whether categories are stored as prototypes, exemplars, or rules, with implications for how they are learned.  ## Details  - **Definition** — Category learning is the acquisition of knowledge that supports classifying novel items and generalizing learned properties. - **Theories** — Prototype theory stores averages, exemplar theory store

body_head: # Category Pages  ## Summary Category pages list every article in a category, usually generated from tags or frontmatter so the list never goes stale.  ## Details - They answer the question 'what does this wiki have on X?' and are the main alternative to full-text search for browsing. - Category pages succeed when the category vocabulary is clean — that is why they depend on tags-practice and tag-hygiene. - For mykb, category pages are hub pages fed by the tag set, and their completeness is a health-dashboard signal.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/tags-practice|Tags Practice]] - [[wiki/concepts/hub-pages|Hub Pages]] - [[wiki/data-storage/indexes-wiki|Indexes]] - [[wiki/concepts/topic-pages|

title: Causal Interventions in AI
description: Perturbing internals to test causal roles
body_head: # Causal Interventions in AI  ## Summary Causal interventions edit a model's internal state (activations, weights, tokens) and observe output changes, testing whether a component is causally load-bearing. Where probes and correlational analyses can only show that information is present somewhere, interventions show whether a component actually matters: change it and the behavior changes, or it does not.  ## Details - The logic follows experimental design: hold everything fixed, manipulate one variable (a single activation, attention head, or weight), and measure the effect on the outcome. title: Causal Reasoning
description: Inferring and using cause-effect relations to explain, predict, and intervene
body_head: # Causal Reasoning  ## Summary  Causal Reasoning — Inferring and using cause-effect relations to explain, predict, and intervene.  ## Details  - Causal reasoning identifies and exploits cause-effect relations: it explains outcomes, predicts under interventions, and guides action. Philosophical accounts range from regularity and counterfactual dependence to mechanisms; Pearl's causal framework formalizes it with graphs, interventions, and counterfactuals. - Key concepts: correlation is not causation; confounders create spurious associations; randomized experiments identify causes; do-calculus and structural models extend identification to observational data. title: Change Blindness
description: Failure to notice changes in a visual scene across disruptions
body_head: # Change Blindness  ## Summary  Change Blindness — Failure to notice changes in a visual scene across disruptions. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - People miss large changes when a flicker, blink, or cut interrupts the scene. - Shows perception relies on sparse, task-relevant representation. - Flicker paradigm and door studies are classic demonstrations. - Important for eyewitness memory and interface design.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/inattentional-blindness|Inattentional Blindness]] — sibling phenomenon - [[wiki/memory/attention-and-cognition|Attention and Cognition]] — framework - [[wiki/concepts/top-down-

description: Git-based snapshots taken before every mutation so any change can be reverted — the self-improvement safety net
body_head: # Checkpoint & Rollback  ## Summary Checkpointing is the practice of committing a git snapshot before every state mutation, so a failed improvement can be rolled back to the last known-good state. It is what makes autonomous modification safe: you can always undo. RSIS3 wraps git commits in a CheckpointManager; loops call `checkpoint("l4-tune")` etc. before writing new state.  ## Details - **Invariant**: checkpoint-before-mutation — the commit lands *before* the write, so rollback targets a verified state. - **Format**: commits use `rsis-checkpoint: <message> [ISO timestamp]` subjects, making them greppable across history. - **Rollback**: `rollback(<hash>)` restores the workspace and hard-

title: Circuit Analysis
description: Mapping the computational circuits a network implements
body_head: # Circuit Analysis  ## Summary Circuit analysis identifies the small subnetworks (circuits) that implement behaviors like induction, addition, or translation. It is the core of mechanistic interpretability: instead of treating the network as an opaque function, circuit analysis decomposes a behavior into the specific attention heads, MLP neurons, and connections that compute it, then verifies the decomposition causally.  ## Details - A circuit is a minimal, task-specific subgraph of the full network: a set of components and the connections between them that suffices to implement a behavior. title: Circuit Tracing
description: Identifying the specific components implementing a behavior
body_head: # Circuit Tracing  ## Summary Circuit tracing locates the attention heads, MLPs, and connections that implement a given behavior. It is the method half of circuit analysis: given a behavior you want to explain, tracing produces the specific causal path — which components, in which order, carrying which information — that implements it.  ## Details - The standard toolkit combines three families of evidence. Attribution methods (gradient-based or attention-based) generate candidate components cheaply and at scale, ranking heads and neurons by how much they influence the output. title: Cognitive Endurance
description: The capacity to sustain demanding cognitive work over time
body_head: # Cognitive Endurance  ## Summary  Cognitive endurance is the capacity to maintain performance on demanding mental tasks over extended periods despite fatigue. It matters because real intellectual work — debugging, research, decision-making — is sustained, not sprint-like. Endurance is shaped by effort regulation, breaks, and task structure, and it degrades in characteristic ways that are measurable.  ## Details  - **Definition** — Endurance refers to how long and how well a person sustains effortful cognition before performance, accuracy, or willingness to continue declines. - **Mechanisms** — Fatigue, motivation, and attentional resources interact: perceived effort rises, and the cost-be

title: Cognitive Load
description: The demand placed on working memory by a task or context
body_head: # Cognitive Load  ## Summary Cognitive load is the amount of mental resources a task consumes; overload degrades judgment and recall. It matters because agent context windows have the same property: too much irrelevant information reduces performance. Managing load is context management in cognitive terms.  ## Details - Sources: task complexity, information density, and interference. - Symptoms in agents: dropped instructions, degraded answers, repetition. - Mitigation: summarization, retrieval, and pinning critical items. - Open questions: measuring load in LLM context windows directly. - Cognitive load is the total mental effort imposed on working memory by a task, split into intrinsic l

title: Cognitive Reflection Test

body_head: # Cognitive Reflection Test  ## Summary  Cognitive Reflection Test — Short test of overriding intuitive wrong answers with deliberation. title: Coherent Extrapolated Volition

body_head: # Coherent Extrapolated Volition  ## Summary Coherent extrapolated volition (CEV) is the hypothetical outcome of humans becoming more informed, more intelligent, and more coherent about what they want. title: Conflict-of-Interest Editing

body_head: # Conflict-of-Interest Editing  ## Summary Conflict-of-interest editing happens when an editor has a personal or financial stake in the article's subject — their employer, product, or client.  ## Details - COI does not make edits automatically wrong; it makes them structurally unreliable and subject to disclosure. - The convention is disclosure first, then review: COI edits are allowed but flagged and checked by others. - For mykb, coi-editing is disclosed in edit summaries and its outputs are priority-reviewed.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/coi-editing|Conflict-of-Interest Editing]] - [[wiki/concepts/paid-editing|Paid Editing]] - [[wiki/concepts/self-promotion|Self-Promotion]] - [[wiki/co

title: Cold Topics

title: Compute Governance

body_head: # Compute Governance  ## Summary Compute governance is the idea that AI's most measurable input — compute — can serve as the handle for oversight: registry of large training runs, export controls on chips, and compute-based thresholds for safety requirements. Sastry et al.'s 2020 analysis made the proposal concrete.  ## Details - **Why compute** — compute is easier to measure and track than models or data, and capability correlates with it. - **Levers** — registration thresholds, licensing of training clusters, chip export controls, and 'compute provenance' for model releases. - **Trade-offs** — over-regulation of compute can entrench incumbents and drive runs underground; thresholds must

title: Conceptual Blending
description: Combining elements from multiple mental spaces into new meaning
body_head: # Conceptual Blending  ## Summary  Conceptual blending is the cognitive operation of combining elements from two or more mental spaces to create a new, integrated meaning that has its own structure. It matters because it explains how novel ideas, metaphors, and jokes emerge from familiar material. Blending is pervasive in language and thought, from compound words to scientific analogies.  ## Details  - **Definition** — A blend projects selected structure from input spaces into a new space with emergent properties neither input possesses alone. - **Mechanism** — Cross-space mapping aligns counterparts; selective projection picks what enters the blend; composition and completion elaborate it

title: Conditional Reasoning

title: Confabulation
description: Producing plausible but fabricated explanations without intent to deceive
body_head: # Confabulation  ## Summary Confabulation is when an agent generates a coherent, confident account that does not match reality — often filling memory gaps after the fact. It differs from deliberate lying because the agent believes the account: the story is constructed to be plausible, not to deceive. In LLM agents it overlaps with hallucination and is a key evaluation target, because a system that confabulates about its own history corrupts its learning loop.  ## Details - The cognitive-science root is human memory: people routinely fill gaps in episodic recall with plausible reconstructions and later cannot distinguish the reconstruction from the memory. title: Confidence Intervals
description: Range estimates that quantify sampling uncertainty
body_head: # Confidence Intervals  ## Summary  Confidence Intervals — Range estimates that quantify sampling uncertainty. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - A 95% CI is a procedure property: repeated sampling covers the parameter 95% of the time. - Wider intervals mean less precision, not less truth. - Intervals carry more information than p-values. - Visualized as error bars; misreading is common.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/effect-size-interpretation|Effect Size Interpretation]] — interval use - [[wiki/questions/uncertainty-communication|Uncertainty Communication]] — presentation - [[wiki/concepts/bayesian-updating-pract

title: Consequentialism for AI
description: Evaluating AI actions by their consequences
body_head: # Consequentialism for AI  ## Summary Consequentialist AI ethics judges actions by outcomes: maximize expected good, minimize expected harm. It is the default frame in alignment — utility functions, expected-value reasoning, and reward optimization are all consequentialist machinery — but it faces severe measurement problems: consequences are hard to enumerate, hard to weigh, and hard to predict.  ## Details - The core structure is simple: an action is right insofar as its consequences are good. title: Constraint Logic Programming
description: Logic programming extended with constraint solving over domains
body_head: # Constraint Logic Programming  ## Summary Constraint logic programming (CLP) embeds constraint solving into logic programming: variables can be constrained over domains (integers, reals, booleans) and the solver prunes search. It matters because it cleanly combines declarative rules with efficient domain reasoning. Prolog systems like SWI-Prolog and SICStus ship CLP libraries.  ## Details - The key mechanism is propagation: instead of enumerating values, the program states relationships between variables, and each constraint's propagator removes impossible values from the variables' domains. It matters because many agent tasks are really constraint problems in disguise, and RSIS3 explicitly tracks constraints as first-class objects that bound agent behavior.  ## Details - **Formulation**: variables, domains, and constraints; a solution is a complete, consistent assignment. - **Search**: backtracking with constraint propagation (forward checking, arc consistency) prunes dead branches. - Variants: binary vs. global constraints, optimization (soft constra

title: Dated Claims

title: Deadband Control
description: Hysteresis thresholds that keep a controller silent inside a target band and reactive outside it
body_head: # Deadband Control  ## Summary Deadband control is the practice of defining a band of acceptable values inside which a controller does nothing, and reacting only when the signal leaves the band. The hysteresis prevents chattering — the loop equivalent of a thermostat switching on and off every second. RSIS3 uses deadbands pervasively: L4's `[target_success_low, target_success_high]`, L6's `[shrink_below, grow_above]`, L7's widening/narrowing of the L4 band, and L9's tuning of the L6 band.  ## Details - **Why a band instead of a setpoint**: a single target invites oscillation around it; a band gives the system permission to do nothing. - **Narrowing**: when the controller stalls (silent whi

title: Debiasing Techniques
description: Methods for reducing or counteracting cognitive biases
body_head: # Debiasing Techniques  ## Summary  Debiasing techniques are interventions that reduce the influence of cognitive biases on judgment and decision-making. They range from individual strategies — considering alternatives, seeking disconfirming evidence — to structural fixes that change the environment or process. They matter because most biases resist pure awareness, so effective debiasing usually changes incentives, defaults, or procedures rather than intentions.  ## Details  - **Definition** — A debiasing technique targets a specific bias or family of biases by altering reasoning, information flow, or decision structure. - **Individual strategies** — Consider-the-opposite, pre-mortems, and

title: Decay Functions

body_head: # Decay Functions  ## Summary Decay functions model how knowledge loses currency over time: exponential decay, half-life models, or step functions for version-validity.  ## Details - They turn 'this is getting stale' into a number: at time t, how much of this article's value should still count. - Decay parameters are topic-specific — Android API knowledge decays faster than git fundamentals. - For mykb, decay functions are the engine under recency-weighting and the timeliness score.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/decay-functions|Decay Functions]] - [[wiki/concepts/half-life-knowledge|Half-Life of Knowledge]] - [[wiki/concepts/recency-weighting|Recency Weighting]] - [[wiki/concepts/freshness

title: Deceptive Alignment

title: Deep Dives
description: Long, thorough treatments of a single topic
body_head: # Deep Dives  ## Summary Deep dives are long-form articles that exhaust a single topic: mechanism, history, tradeoffs, examples, and open questions.  ## Details - They earn their length by depth of analysis, not by padding — every section should add understanding a shorter article lacks. - Deep dives are the most expensive articles to maintain and should be reserved for stable, important topics. - For mykb, deep dives are the top of the content hierarchy and are reviewed for accuracy before any other article.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/longforms|Longforms]] - [[wiki/concepts/deep-dives|Deep Dives]] - [[wiki/data-storage/case-studies-wiki|Case Studies]] - [[wiki/concepts/keystone-article

title: Defeasible Reasoning
description: Reasoning with conclusions that can be withdrawn given new evidence
body_head: # Defeasible Reasoning  ## Summary Defeasible reasoning allows conclusions to be retracted when counter-evidence or stronger arguments appear. It matters because real-world knowledge is exception-laden and agents must revise. It is the applied face of non-monotonic logic.  ## Details - Arguments have strength; defeaters can overturn conclusions. - Default rules express 'normally, unless...' knowledge. - Essential for belief revision in dynamic environments. - Open questions: defeasible reasoning in LLM argument generation.  ## Related - [[wiki/llm-agents/self-reflection-agents|Self-Reflection Agents]] — revising one's own conclusions - [[wiki/concepts/non-monotonic-logic|Non-Monotonic Logi

title: Delete Proposal
description: A structured proposal to remove an article
body_head: # Delete Proposal  ## Summary A delete proposal records the case for removing an article entirely: what it is, why deletion beats archival or merge, and who approved it.  ## Details - Deletion is the least reversible curation action, so proposals demand the highest bar and a visible approval trail. - The proposal should also name the deletion's graph impact — every inbound link must be handled first. - For mykb, delete proposals follow deletion-criteria and are reviewed before the article is actually removed.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/deletion-criteria|Deletion Criteria]] - [[wiki/concepts/delete-proposal|Delete Proposal]] - [[wiki/concepts/archival-criteria|Archival Criteria]] - [[wik

title: Deletion Criteria
description: When an article is removed entirely rather than archived or demoted
body_head: # Deletion Criteria  ## Summary Deletion criteria cover the narrow cases where removal is right: duplicate content whose merge is complete, pages that were never real articles, or material that is actively wrong with no salvageable value.  ## Details - Deletion should be the rarest lifecycle action because it destroys provenance; when in doubt, archive instead. - Proposed deletions should pass a review step and leave a record (a delete-proposal) so the decision can be audited. - For mykb, deletion proposals are tracked like merge and split proposals, with a review queue before anything is actually removed.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/archival-criteria|Archival Criteria]] - [[wiki/concept

title: Demotion Criteria
description: The conditions under which a full article drops back to stub status
body_head: # Demotion Criteria  ## Summary Demotion criteria describe when an article loses growing status: it can no longer be verified, its sources rot, or its claims become unsupported by current evidence.  ## Details - Demotion is not punishment — it is honesty about the article's current state, and it routes the article back into the promotion queue once fixed. - Automatic demotion triggers include link-rot, flagged factual errors, and failed freshness reviews. - For mykb, demotion keeps full-article-ratio honest: a stale full article is worse than an honest stub.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/promotion-readiness|Promotion Readiness]] - [[wiki/concepts/archival-criteria|Archival Criteria]] - [[w

title: Deontology for AI
description: Rules-based ethics for AI systems
body_head: # Deontology for AI  ## Summary Deontological AI ethics binds systems to rules and duties rather than optimizing outcomes. Where consequentialism asks "what produces the best results?", deontology asks "what is the right thing to do, regardless of consequences?" For AI this translates into hard constraints: do not deceive, do not harm, do not violate permissions — rules that hold even when violating them would score higher on the objective.  ## Details - The appeal is predictability and rights protection. Rule-governed systems have stable, auditable behavior: an observer can check whether the system obeyed its rules without reconstructing its full consequence calculus. Rules also protect i

title: Dependency Attacks
description: Compromising AI systems through their dependencies
body_head: # Dependency Attacks  ## Summary Dependency attacks exploit trusted libraries or services that AI systems rely on, from ML frameworks to vector stores. They are supply-chain attacks aimed at the dependency graph: compromise a package the system imports, and you inherit code execution inside the system's trust boundary without touching the system's own code.  ## Details - The attack surface is huge because AI systems stack many layers of dependencies: base images and operating-system packages, Python and Node package registries, ML frameworks and model-serving runtimes, embedding and vector-store clients, and the data pipelines that feed training and retrieval. title: Distribution Shift in AI
description: Deployment data differing from training data
body_head: # Distribution Shift in AI  ## Summary Distribution shift is the mismatch between the data a model saw in training and the data it meets in deployment. It is the rule, not the exception: the world moves, users change, formats drift, and any deployed model is eventually operating on inputs that its training distribution did not anticipate — which is why a model's in-distribution benchmark score routinely overstates its real-world performance.  ## Details - Shift comes in identifiable flavors. Covariate shift: the input distribution changes while the input-output relationship stays the same (new photo styles, new document layouts). title: Distributional Robustness
description: Performance guarantees across distribution families
body_head: # Distributional Robustness  ## Summary Distributional robustness aims for acceptable performance across a defined family of shifted distributions, not just the training one. Instead of optimizing for the single training distribution and hoping the world matches it, the robust approach optimizes for the worst case within a specified uncertainty set — accepting some in-distribution loss in exchange for a guarantee that performance will not collapse when the world shifts.  ## Details - The formalism is distributionally robust optimization (DRO): minimize loss under the worst-case distribution within an ambiguity set around the training distribution. title: Divided Attention
description: Processing multiple tasks or streams simultaneously
body_head: # Divided Attention  ## Summary  Divided attention is the ability, or attempt, to process multiple tasks or information streams at the same time. It matters because human attention is a limited resource: dividing it costs accuracy, speed, and memory, especially when tasks compete for the same cognitive machinery. Understanding those limits explains why multitasking underperforms focused work and when it is safe.  ## Details  - **Definition** — Dividing attention means allocating limited processing resources across concurrent tasks or streams rather than focusing them on one. - **Resource limits** — Two tasks that draw on the same modality or process — two verbal streams, two motor plans —

body_head: # Dogfooding  ## Summary Dogfooding is the practice of using one's own product in real work so its flaws surface naturally. For AI systems it means the improvement loop runs on itself — the wiki would be curated with the wiki's own tools, the agent uses its own agent stack — turning incidents into fixes.  ## Details - **Why it works** — real usage exposes problems no synthetic test can: friction, broken links, missing features. - **Eat-your-own-dog-food lineage** — self-hosting culture in compilers generalized to products. - **Agent/AI form** — dogfooding doubles as self-evaluation: the system is its own first production user. - **Risk** — dogfooding biases the product toward the maker's u

title: Dual Process Theory
description: Fast intuitive System 1 and slow deliberate System 2 reasoning
body_head: # Dual Process Theory  ## Summary Dual process theory distinguishes fast, automatic, intuitive processing (System 1) from slow, effortful, deliberate reasoning (System 2). It matters because it predicts when agents will be efficient and when they will err. LLM agents often emulate both: quick generation plus explicit verification.  ## Details - System 1: pattern matching, heuristics — cheap but biased. - System 2: search, verification, reflection — expensive but corrigible. - Agent design maps to it: fast draft, then deliberate check. - Open questions: when to trigger System 2, and how to measure the cost-benefit. - Dual process theory divides thinking into two systems: System 1 is fast, a

body_head: # Dual-Use Research  ## Summary Dual-use research is work whose findings enable both constructive and destructive applications — synthetic biology, cyber exploits, or general-purpose AI methods. Governance seeks to preserve benefits while restricting the most dangerous applications.  ## Details - **Canonical case** — gain-of-function virology: understanding pandemic potential requires making pathogens more transmissible. - **AI dimension** — capability research (self-improvement, persuasion, autonomy) is dual-use by nature. - **Screening** — publication review, tiered access, and expert panels classify risk before release. - **Responsible scaling link** — frontier labs treat dual-use capab

title: Early Stopping
description: Ending training when validation performance degrades
body_head: # Early Stopping  ## Summary Early stopping halts training when a validation metric stops improving, trading a bit of training-set fit for generalization. It is the simplest effective regularizer in deep learning: instead of deciding a priori how many epochs to run, watch a held-out validation metric and stop when it degrades, keeping the best checkpoint seen so far.  ## Details - The mechanism is a direct measurement of the bias-variance tradeoff. During training, the model first improves on both training and validation loss as it learns real structure; eventually it starts memorizing training-set idiosyncrasies, and validation loss turns upward while training loss keeps falling. body_head: # Edit Warring  ## Summary Edit warring is repeatedly reverting another editor's changes to win control of an article — the same edit going back and forth.  ## Details - It is harmful even when the 'correct' side wins, because it burns goodwill and produces unstable content. - The remedy is process, not force: stop editing, discuss, and route through dispute resolution; the three-revert rule sets the boundary. - For mykb, edit warring on an article triggers protection and moves the dispute to the consensus process.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/edit-warring|Edit Warring]] - [[wiki/concepts/3rr-rule|Three-Revert Rule]] - [[wiki/concepts/reverts-wiki|Reverts]] - [[wiki/concepts/dispute-resol

body_head: # Elicitation Techniques  ## Summary Elicitation techniques extract knowledge a model may possess but not show: careful prompting, probing, and behavioral tests. body_head: # Emergence in LLMs  ## Summary Emergence refers to capabilities that seem to appear suddenly at a scale threshold, rather than growing smoothly with parameters. title: Episodic Memory

body_head: # Episodic Memory  ## Summary Episodic memory stores concrete episodes: what happened, when, and with what outcome. It matters because agents need to recall their own history to learn from it. RSIS3 pulses and mykb session notes are episodic memory in practice.  ## Details - Episodes include context, actions, observations, and outcome. - Query patterns: 'what did we try last time and why did it fail?' - Linked to temporal analysis for rising/falling topic detection. - Open questions: granularity of episodes and retention policy. - Episodic memory stores specific events with their time, place, and context — the 'what happened when' layer of memory. - It contrasts with semantic memory: episo

body_head: # Epistemology Foundations  ## Summary  Epistemology Foundations — The philosophical study of knowledge: its nature, sources, and limits.  ## Details  - Epistemology asks what knowledge is, what can be known, and how belief becomes justified. The classical analysis treats knowledge as justified true belief; Gettier cases show justification plus truth can still fall short, spurring refinements (reliabilism, virtue epistemology, and externalist accounts). - Core questions: the sources of knowledge (perception, introspection, reason, testimony, memory), the structure of justification (foundationalism versus coherentism), and the limits of knowledge (skepticism, uncertainty). - Worked example:

title: Eval Contamination
description: Any leakage that corrupts evaluation validity
body_head: # Eval Contamination  ## Summary Eval contamination covers all ways evaluation validity is corrupted: leaked data, gamed metrics, or feedback loops from eval to training. An eval is only as good as its integrity — if the test data appears in training, if the metric can be optimized without the capability, or if the eval's existence changes the model's behavior, the score stops measuring what it claims to measure.  ## Details - The data form is train-test leakage: benchmark items included in pretraining or fine-tuning corpora, directly or in paraphrase. title: Evaluation Frameworks for AI

body_head: # Evaluation Frameworks for AI  ## Summary Evaluation frameworks organize how models are tested: which capabilities, which datasets, which metrics, which thresholds. A framework turns "is this model good?" into a reproducible protocol — defined tasks with known difficulty, standard metrics with agreed interpretation, and explicit decision thresholds that map scores to actions like "deploy", "monitor", or "do not release".  ## Details - A framework has four layers. title: Event Segmentation
description: Parsing continuous experience into discrete events
body_head: # Event Segmentation  ## Summary  Event segmentation is the perceptual process of dividing continuous experience into discrete events with beginnings and ends. It matters because event boundaries organize memory: what happens around a boundary is remembered better, and segmentation skill predicts memory and learning. Segmentation is automatic, driven by prediction error when the environment changes.  ## Details  - **Definition** — Segmenters identify boundaries where one activity ends and another begins, chunking streams of behavior into meaningful units. - **Mechanism** — Boundaries tend to coincide with prediction errors — moments when unfolding activity violates expectations and the sit

title: Evergreen Articles
description: Articles that stay accurate without frequent updates
body_head: # Evergreen Articles  ## Summary Evergreen articles are written so they stay accurate: they describe durable mechanisms and principles rather than current versions and news.  ## Details - Evergreen is a writing discipline — phrasing claims to survive version changes ('the current release as of 2026') keeps a page alive. - Evergreen articles still need review, but on the longest cadence, which makes them the cheapest pages to own. - For mykb, evergreen articles are the backbone of the wiki and the target state most promotions aim for.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/timely-articles|Timely Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/evergreen-articles|Evergreen Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/dated-claims|Dated

title: Evidence and Justification
description: What counts as evidence for a claim and when it justifies belief
body_head: # Evidence and Justification  ## Summary  Evidence and Justification — What counts as evidence for a claim and when it justifies belief.  ## Details  - Evidence is information that bears on the truth of a claim; justification is the standing evidence gives to belief. Internalist views require the believer to have access to reasons; externalist views (reliabilism) accept reliable processes even without access — the distinction drives how much trust we place in intuition versus measurement. - Evidence varies in strength: direct observation, testimony, statistical data, and mechanism-based explanations each justify differently. Bayesian epistemology formalizes evidence as likelihood ratios th

title: Evidence Hierarchy
description: Ordering of evidence types by resistance to bias
body_head: # Evidence Hierarchy  ## Summary  Evidence Hierarchy — Ordering of evidence types by resistance to bias. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Typical order: meta-analyses, RCTs, cohort, case-control, case series, opinion. - Randomization controls confounds but limits generalizability. - Hierarchies are decision aids, not proofs. - Guides evidence evaluation in medicine, policy, and knowledge systems.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/evidence-pyramid|Evidence Pyramid]] — visual form - [[wiki/concepts/systematic-review|Systematic Review]] — method - [[wiki/concepts/replication-crisis|Replication Crisis]] — limits of rank

body_head: # Evidence Pyramid  ## Summary  Evidence Pyramid — Visual hierarchy ranking study designs by evidentiary strength. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Pyramids place systematic reviews/meta-analyses on top, expert opinion at the base. - Useful for teaching but oversimplifies: design alone does not guarantee quality. - Question fit matters more than raw rank. - Companion to the evidence-hierarchy concept.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/evidence-hierarchy|Evidence Hierarchy]] — the ranking idea - [[wiki/concepts/systematic-review|Systematic Review]] — top tier - [[wiki/concepts/meta-analysis-methods|Meta Analysis Meth

title: Examples Needed

body_head: # Examples Needed  ## Summary Examples-needed marks articles whose claims are abstract but demonstrable — the concept needs a worked example to be usable.  ## Details - A missing example is a usability gap, not a correctness gap; the flag usually appears at promotion review. - The flag note should say which part needs the example, so the add lands where readers stumble. - For mykb, examples-needed flags are common on full articles about protocols and patterns, and they feed the content-score.  ## Related - [[wiki/data-storage/examples-in-wiki|Examples in the Wiki]] - [[wiki/concepts/examples-needed|Examples Needed]] - [[wiki/ai-ml/content-score|Content Score]] - [[wiki/concepts/promotion-r

title: Executive Function
description: The cognitive control layer that plans, prioritizes, and inhibits actions
body_head: # Executive Function  ## Summary Executive function is the set of high-level cognitive controls — planning, working memory management, inhibition, and task switching — that organize lower-level behavior. It matters because an agent without it reacts; with it, it executes strategy. In agent terms it maps to the orchestrator or planner role.  ## Details - Core abilities: goal maintenance, prioritization, stopping a wrong course, switching tasks. - Failure modes: perseveration (stuck on one approach) and goal neglect. - RSIS3 relevance: the executive planner and L3 goal direction are executive functions. - Open questions: how to measure executive control quality in agents. - Executive functio

title: Exemplar Theory
description: Categorization by similarity to stored individual instances
body_head: # Exemplar Theory  ## Summary  Exemplar theory holds that categories are represented by stored individual instances — exemplars — and that new items are categorized by their similarity to those memories. It matters because it explains subtle categorization behavior that averaged prototypes cannot: sensitivity to typicality, variability, and correlations among features. It also connects categorization directly to memory.  ## Details  - **Definition** — Instead of storing a single category average, the mind stores many examples; classification compares a novel item against all of them. - **Similarity** — Classification sums or weights similarity to stored exemplars, so a category is effectiv

title: Exfiltration Evals
description: Testing whether agents exfiltrate data or models
body_head: # Exfiltration Evals  ## Summary Exfiltration evals test whether an agent can copy protected data or weights out of its environment.  ## Details - Exfiltration evals test whether an agent can copy protected data or weights out of its environment. - Exfiltration is the mechanism for model theft and data leaks. - Defenses: egress controls, monitoring, and sandboxing. - RSIS3 relevance: sandboxed workers with bounded scopes reduce exfiltration surface.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/self-replication-evals|Self-Replication Evals]] — the replication twin - [[wiki/syntheses/containment-strategies|Containment Strategies]] — the defense - [[wiki/agent-systems/agent-sandboxing|Agent Sandboxing]] — t

title: Existential Risk
description: Risks of extinction or permanent collapse of civilization
body_head: # Existential Risk  ## Summary Existential risk (x-risk) is risk that humanity's potential is permanently destroyed, typically via extinction or irreversible collapse.  ## Details - Existential risk (x-risk) is risk that humanity's potential is permanently destroyed, typically via extinction or irreversible collapse. - AI x-risk arguments combine capability forecasts with misalignment likelihood. - X-risk framing motivates urgency and governs research priorities. - RSIS3 relevance: the wiki's safety cluster organizes x-risk concepts for the graph.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/x-risk-frameworks|X-Risk Frameworks]] — the analysis methods - [[wiki/concepts/catastrophic-misalignment|Catastrop
