title: Expected Utility
description: The formal framework for decisions under uncertainty
body_head: # Expected Utility  ## Summary Expected utility theory represents preferences as utility over outcomes, maximized in expectation under uncertainty.  ## Details - Expected utility theory represents preferences as utility over outcomes, maximized in expectation under uncertainty. - It is the standard formal frame in economics, game theory, and AI value design. - Violations (ambiguity aversion, risk attitudes) motivate bounded and robust variants. - RSIS3 relevance: utility-function concepts in the graph sit on this foundation.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/utility-functions|Utility Functions]] — the AI representation - [[wiki/concepts/expected-value-reasoning|Expected Value Reasoning]] — the

title: Expected Value Reasoning
description: Deciding by probability-weighted outcomes
body_head: # Expected Value Reasoning  ## Summary Expected value reasoning multiplies each outcome's value by its probability and sums, choosing the highest total. It is the standard rational decision rule: instead of comparing best cases, worst cases, or the most likely scenario, it weighs every possibility by how likely it is and how much it is worth, then acts on the best weighted average.  ## Details - The calculation is deceptively simple: EV = sum of P(outcome) × V(outcome) over all outcomes. Its power is that it forces the decision-maker to enumerate outcomes explicitly, assign probabilities honestly, and price values — the discipline of writing down the model is often worth more than the arit

title: Expert Systems
description: Classical rule-based systems encoding human expertise in a domain
body_head: # Expert Systems  ## Summary Expert systems encode domain expertise as a knowledge base of rules plus an inference engine (typically forward or backward chaining) to apply them. They matter because they were the first successful applied AI and still define the knowledge-engineering trade-offs. Modern agents reuse the pattern with learned knowledge.  ## Details - Components: knowledge base, inference engine, explanation facility. The knowledge base holds facts and production rules ("IF the patient has X and Y THEN conclude Z with confidence 0.8"); the inference engine decides which rules to apply and in what order; and the explanation facility records the chain of fired rules so a user can

title: Explainers
description: Articles whose goal is understanding rather than procedure
body_head: # Explainers  ## Summary Explainers make a concept understandable: how it works, why it exists, what it trades off — with analogy, mechanism, and example.  ## Details - The success criterion is reader comprehension, not completeness; a short explainer that lands beats a long one that wanders. - Explainers pair with how-tos: understanding (explainer) and doing (how-to) reinforce each other and should link. - For mykb, explainers are the default format for full articles about concepts, with comprehension-score as their quality signal.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/primers|Primers]] - [[wiki/concepts/explainers|Explainers]] - [[wiki/concepts/how-to-articles|How-To Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts

title: Exploration-Exploitation
description: The trade-off between trying new options and using known good ones
body_head: # Exploration-Exploitation  ## Summary Every agent faces the exploration-exploitation trade-off: exploit what is known to work, or explore for something better. It matters because too little exploration stagnates and too much wastes budget. Bandit algorithms are the simplest formal treatment.  ## Details - Exploration collects information; exploitation collects reward. - Strategies: epsilon-greedy, optimistic initialization, UCB. - RSIS3 relevance: L2/L3 try new strategies only within test gates. - Open questions: exploration budgets in LLM action spaces.  ## Related - [[wiki/agent-systems/planning-systems|Planning Systems]] — planning as informed exploitation - [[wiki/concepts/multi-armed

title: External Links Policy
description: Rules for linking outside the wiki
body_head: # External Links Policy  ## Summary The external links policy governs when and how articles link outside the wiki: sources in references, official docs, and curated further-reading are allowed; spammy or tangential links are not.  ## Details - External links are the wiki's interface with the wider web, so they carry trust and maintenance costs that internal links do not. - The policy should require a reason for every external link and prohibit link-stuffing and promotional links. - For mykb, external links are concentrated in reference blocks and further-reading, keeping prose free of interstitial URLs.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/internal-links-policy|Internal Links Policy]] - [[wiki/co

title: Extraction Attacks
description: Recovering training data from model outputs
body_head: # Extraction Attacks  ## Summary Extraction attacks prompt or query models to recover memorized training data.  ## Details - Extraction attacks prompt or query models to recover memorized training data. - Success depends on memorization, prompting skill, and model size. - Membership inference is the weaker cousin: just detecting whether an example was in training. - RSIS3 relevance: any knowledge store with sensitive records faces extraction-style risks.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/training-data-extraction|Training Data Extraction]] — the same problem - [[wiki/concepts/training-data-memorization|Training Data Memorization]] — the enabler - [[wiki/concepts/privacy-attacks-llm|Privacy Atta

title: Fat-Tailed Distributions
description: Distributions where extreme events are more likely than normal
body_head: # Fat-Tailed Distributions  ## Summary Fat-tailed distributions assign meaningful probability to extreme events, unlike Gaussians.  ## Details - Fat-tailed distributions assign meaningful probability to extreme events, unlike Gaussians. - AI capability growth and downside risks are widely argued to be fat-tailed. - Fat tails undermine point forecasts and demand robust, precautionary decisions. - RSIS3 relevance: the graph's forecasting pages carry this statistical caveat.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/tail-risks|Tail Risks]] — the event-level view - [[wiki/concepts/worst-case-reasoning|Worst-Case Reasoning]] — the decision response - [[wiki/concepts/capability-forecasting|Capability Foreca

title: Feature Double-Counting
description: The same concept appearing as multiple separate features
body_head: # Feature Double-Counting  ## Summary Feature double-counting is when a concept is split across several dictionary features, so the decomposition over-counts it.  ## Details - Feature double-counting is when a concept is split across several dictionary features, so the decomposition over-counts it. - It distorts interpretability claims and any downstream use of feature attributions. - Detection and merging of duplicate features is an open research problem. - RSIS3 relevance: duplicate graph nodes are the knowledge-graph analogue.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/sae-research|SAE Research]] — where it is observed - [[wiki/concepts/dictionary-learning-ai|Dictionary Learning for AI]] — the frame

title: Feature Visualization
description: Visualizing what network features detect
body_head: # Feature Visualization  ## Summary Feature visualization optimizes inputs that maximally activate a neuron or feature, producing images of what it detects. It is the oldest intuitive tool of interpretability: if you want to know what a unit responds to, search input space for the pattern that lights it up most, and the resulting image is the unit's "preferred stimulus" made visible.  ## Details - The method: take the model's weights, pick a target unit (a neuron, channel, or dictionary feature), and run gradient ascent on a synthetic input to maximize that unit's activation — optionally with regularization to keep the result naturalistic. Early work used random noise and produced recogniz

title: AI Fingerprinting
description: Identifying the model that produced content
body_head: # AI Fingerprinting  ## Summary AI fingerprinting identifies which model generated a piece of content, via statistical patterns or embedded marks.  ## Details - AI fingerprinting identifies which model generated a piece of content, via statistical patterns or embedded marks. - It supports attribution, copyright, and abuse investigations. - Accuracy varies; strong fingerprints are hard to remove. - RSIS3 relevance: fingerprinting generated notes aids provenance audits.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/watermarking-ai|Watermarking AI Content]] — the marking mechanism - [[wiki/concepts/attribution-ai|Attribution for AI]] — the credit purpose - [[wiki/concepts/content-authentication|Content Authe

title: First-Paragraph Links
description: Linking the most important related concepts early in an article
body_head: # First-Paragraph Links  ## Summary First-paragraph links put the article's most important relationships in the opening prose, where readers and search both look first.  ## Details - A strong first paragraph links the concept to its parent and its key contrast — the two neighbors that frame it. - The convention forces authors to decide early what the article is about, which improves both links and prose. - For mykb, first-paragraph links are encouraged for full articles and count toward the link-score.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/link-placement|Link Placement]] - [[wiki/concepts/link-context|Link Context]] - [[wiki/dev-tools/related-blocks|Related Blocks]] - [[wiki/concepts/discoverabili

title: First-Principles AI
description: Building AI from fundamental reasoning rather than pattern matching or convention
body_head: # First-Principles AI  ## Summary First-principles AI is an approach that designs systems from fundamental laws — logic, causality, utility — rather than from imitating human data or convention. It is often proposed as the safest path to strong AI because every component is derived and inspectable.  ## Details - **Contrast** — data-driven learning finds correlates; first-principles derivation explains why something works. - **Strengths** — auditability, formal guarantees, and resistance to spurious correlations. - **Weaknesses** — known problems resist closed-form solutions; real systems still need learning for perception and common sense. - **Hybrid practice** — modern systems pair learne

title: Fitness Stagnation
description: The plateau signal: generations stop improving, and the meta-tuner responds by raising mutation
body_head: # Fitness Stagnation  ## Summary Fitness stagnation is the state where a population's best fitness stops improving across generations — a plateau that signals the search is stuck in a local region. It is a *signal*, not a failure: the correct response is to explore more. In RSIS3, L8 watches L5's generation-fitness history and, when gains stay under an epsilon for `stagnation_window` generations, raises `l5.mutation_rate` to break out of the plateau.  ## Details - **Detection**: compare consecutive `best_fitness` values in accepted generations; if all gains < ε (default 0.005) over the window, raise mutation. - **Response**: `mutation_rate += mutation_step`, clamped to the registry bounds

title: Forecasting Research
description: Study of how to elicit, aggregate, and score probabilistic forecasts of future events
body_head: # Forecasting Research  ## Summary Forecasting research studies how well people predict future events and how to make them better. Trained forecasters beat experts and institutions, largely through calibration practice, aggregation, and continuous updating. It is the empirical backbone of superforecasting.  ## Details - **Findings** — granular, numeric, regularly-scored forecasts outperform verbal judgments. - **Key practices** — base rates, outside views, updating on evidence, and team aggregation. - **Scoring** — Brier scores measure accuracy; calibration curves check confidence. - **In mykb** — a forecast log with scores trains the skill.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/superforecasters|S

title: Formal Processes
description: Codified procedures for consequential decisions
body_head: # Formal Processes  ## Summary Formal processes are the codified procedures for consequential decisions — policy changes, disputes, bans, and structural actions — with defined steps and records.  ## Details - Their strength is predictability: everyone knows the path, the evidence required, and the appeal route. - Formality has a cost in speed, so the wiki reserves formal process for decisions where reversibility is low. - For mykb, formal processes are the written form of the editorial policy's enforcement half.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/formal-processes|Formal Processes]] - [[wiki/concepts/informal-processes|Informal Processes]] - [[wiki/concepts/rfc-wiki|Requests for Comment]] - [[wi

title: Formal Reasoning
description: Reasoning with explicit rules, such as logic and mathematics
body_head: # Formal Reasoning  ## Summary  Formal Reasoning — Reasoning with explicit rules, such as logic and mathematics. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Formal systems make validity independent of content. - Includes propositional and predicate logic, probability, and math proof. - Humans find formal rules hard to apply consistently (Wason task). - Computers excel where humans struggle; human-computer hybrid is strongest.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/informal-reasoning|Informal Reasoning]] — everyday counterpart - [[wiki/concepts/syllogistic-reasoning|Syllogistic Reasoning]] — classic form - [[wiki/concepts/wason-sele

title: Formal Verification of Agents
description: Mathematically proving properties of agent behavior
body_head: # Formal Verification of Agents  ## Summary Formal verification of agents uses model checking, theorem proving, and specification languages to prove properties such as termination, safety, and goal consistency before deployment. It provides the strongest available guarantees, at the cost of tractability for large learned systems.  ## Details - **Techniques** — model checking finite state spaces, Hoare-style proofs for programmatic agents, and type systems as lightweight verification. - **What can be verified today** — scaffold logic, permission guards, and protocol properties; model internals are harder. - **Bridging learning and logic** — verifiers, monitors, and tripwires attach formal c

title: Forward Chaining
description: Reasoning from known facts toward a goal by applying rules
body_head: # Forward Chaining  ## Summary Forward chaining starts with known facts and repeatedly applies rules whose conditions are satisfied, deriving new facts until the goal is reached or no rule applies. It matters because it is complete, data-driven, and easy to implement — the engine of many expert systems. It is also how agents can reason from observations.  ## Details - Data-driven: all rules fire as their conditions become true. The inference engine maintains a working memory of facts; each cycle it matches rule conditions against the facts, picks a rule whose conditions are satisfied, fires it, and adds the derived fact to working memory. The process continues until the goal is derived, no

title: Forward Models
description: Internal models that predict the next state from current state and action
body_head: # Forward Models  ## Summary  Forward models are internal models that predict the next state of a system — often the body or environment — from the current state and an action. They matter because prediction lets agents compensate for delays, anticipate consequences, and learn from prediction error. Forward models are central to motor control, active perception, and predictive processing accounts of the brain.  ## Details  - **Definition** — A forward model computes an expected next state and sensory outcome given the current state and a candidate action. - **Motor control** — The brain uses forward predictions to compensate for transmission delays, so movements feel immediate despite slow

title: Frames and Slots
description: Structured knowledge representations with named attributes
body_head: # Frames and Slots  ## Summary  Frames and slots are a knowledge representation in which concepts are structures with named attributes — slots — that hold values, defaults, or constraints. They matter because they give reasoning systems and cognitive models a way to organize expectations: a frame for a restaurant has slots for name, cuisine, and price. Frames support default reasoning, inheritance, and expectation-driven processing.  ## Details  - **Definition** — A frame represents a stereotyped situation or concept; slots are its attributes, filled with specific values or filled by defaults. - **Defaults and inheritance** — Slots can carry default values inherited from super-frames, enab

title: Free Energy Principle
description: A theory that self-organizing systems minimize surprise about their world
body_head: # Free Energy Principle  ## Summary The free energy principle (FEP) proposes that adaptive systems act and perceive to minimize variational free energy — a bound on surprise about their sensory world. It matters as an organizing theory for why agents explore, learn, and maintain models. It underpins active inference and predictive processing.  ## Details - The mathematical core: an agent that survives must keep its sensory states within a small set of viable states, which means keeping them unsurprising under its generative model. Since exact surprise is intractable, the agent minimizes variational free energy, an upper bound on surprise that decomposes into accuracy (how well the model pr

title: Freshness Signals
description: The data points that reveal how fresh an article is
body_head: # Freshness Signals  ## Summary Freshness signals are the observable data that reveal an article's currency: source dates, access dates, review timestamps, dated claims, and change history.  ## Details - No single signal is enough — a recently edited article can still cite dead sources, and a never-touched article can be evergreen. - The signals feed the timeliness score and the freshness report that plans refresh-days. - For mykb, freshness signals are collected automatically from frontmatter and reference blocks.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/freshness-signals|Freshness Signals]] - [[wiki/concepts/timeliness-score|Timeliness Score]] - [[wiki/concepts/dated-claims|Dated Claims]] - [[wiki/

title: Frontier Models
description: The most capable AI models at any time
body_head: # Frontier Models  ## Summary Frontier models are the most capable systems at a given moment, usually trained by a handful of labs.  ## Details - Frontier models are the most capable systems at a given moment, usually trained by a handful of labs. - Their capability concentration drives most governance debates and RSP thresholds. - Frontier status is transient; evals must track capability, not marketing. - RSIS3 relevance: capability tracking in the wiki monitors the frontier for context.  ## Related - [[wiki/decisions/frontier-lab-practices|Frontier Lab Practices]] — the institutional side - [[wiki/concepts/responsible-scaling|Responsible Scaling]] — the policy - [[wiki/concepts/dangerous

title: Frozen Articles
description: Articles intentionally locked against changes
body_head: # Frozen Articles  ## Summary Frozen articles are intentionally locked — no edits accepted, usually because they record a settled historical state or are under dispute resolution.  ## Details - Freezing is a governance tool with a cost: frozen articles cannot absorb corrections, so freezes must have an expiry or an appeal path. - Frozen is distinct from stable: stable articles may be edited when needed; frozen articles may not. - For mykb, frozen articles are rare and are tracked with their freeze reason and expiry.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/locked-articles|Locked Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/frozen-articles|Frozen Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/protected-articles|Protected Articles]] -

title: Full Article Ratio
description: The fraction of wiki articles that have reached growing status
body_head: # Full Article Ratio  ## Summary Full article ratio is the count of growing-status articles divided by total articles — the wiki's depth indicator.  ## Details - It is the complement story to stub-ratio: a healthy mature wiki has a high full ratio, while an acquisition phase naturally lowers it. - Ratio alone hides absolute depth, so it is reported with the absolute counts of fulls and stubs. - For mykb, this ratio is the headline number for promotion passes: a curation sprint should move it without sacrificing stub velocity.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/stub-ratio|Stub Ratio]] - [[wiki/concepts/growth-ratio|Growth Ratio]] - [[wiki/concepts/promotion-checklist|Promotion Checklist]] - [[wi

title: Further Reading
description: Curated links for going deeper beyond cited sources
body_head: # Further Reading  ## Summary Further Reading lists optional material — books, papers, guides — that a reader can explore beyond what the article cites.  ## Details - It is distinct from References: further reading is not load-bearing evidence, so it follows looser (but still vetted) quality rules. - The list should be curated, not exhaustive; five excellent entries beat twenty marginal ones. - For mykb, further reading entries are external links governed by the external-links policy.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/see-also|See Also]] - [[wiki/data-storage/reference-lists|Reference Lists]] - [[wiki/concepts/external-links-policy|External Links Policy]] - [[wiki/concepts/further-reading|Furt

title: Generalization Issues
description: The cluster of problems in moving from training to deployment
body_head: # Generalization Issues  ## Summary Generalization issues are the many ways performance fails to transfer: overfitting, shortcuts, distribution shift, and goal misgeneralization. They are the central technical weakness of learned systems — a model that only performs well on training-like inputs is not actually solving the problem, and the failure modes differ enough that each needs its own detection and mitigation.  ## Details - Overfitting is the classic form: the model memorizes training-set idiosyncrasies instead of the underlying regularity, so validation and deployment performance collapse as the data diverges. It is detected by the train-validation gap and mitigated by regularization

title: Generative Models
description: Models that capture how data are generated, enabling prediction and synthesis
body_head: # Generative Models  ## Summary  Generative Models — Models that capture how data are generated, enabling prediction and synthesis. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - A generative model p(x) or p(x|z) explains how observations arise from latent causes. - Used for simulation, counterfactual reasoning, and representation learning. - Contrast with discriminative models that only draw boundaries. - In cognitive science, the brain is cast as a generative model of the world.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/model-based-cognition|Model Based Cognition]] — cognitive framing - [[wiki/concepts/bayesian-brain|Bayesian Brain]] —

title: Global Catastrophic Risk
description: Risks that could harm civilization worldwide
body_head: # Global Catastrophic Risk  ## Summary Global catastrophic risk (GCR) is risk of harm severe enough to degrade civilization worldwide but not necessarily end it. The concept carves out a class of threats distinct from ordinary disasters: pandemics, nuclear war, climate tipping points, and advanced AI all share the property that their consequences would be measured in the loss of civilization's capacity, not merely in lives or dollars.  ## Details - The defining feature is global scale and systemic degradation: a GCR event destroys or severely damages the institutions, infrastructure, and social fabric that recovery depends on, so its harm is qualitatively different from a large but contain

title: Goal Content Thesis
description: Claims about the structure and content of learned goals
body_head: # Goal Content Thesis  ## Summary The goal content thesis concerns what learned optimizers' goals actually look like: simple, convergent, or entangled with training data. It is the empirical question behind alignment theory — not "how should goals be specified?" but "given how learning actually works, what kind of goals will a learned system end up with?" The answer determines which alignment problems are real and which are theoretical.  ## Details - One pole of the debate holds that optimized goals are simple and convergent: a system trained to pursue any goal at all will, under enough optimization pressure, settle into goal-directed behavior with a small set of near-universal instrumenta

title: Goal-Directed Policies
description: Policies that robustly optimize a learned objective
body_head: # Goal-Directed Policies  ## Summary Goal-directed policies are trained policies that behave as if optimizing a coherent objective across states.  ## Details - Goal-directed policies are trained policies that behave as if optimizing a coherent objective across states. - RL agents often approximate goal-directedness even when no explicit utility function was given. - Measuring policy goal-directedness helps predict out-of-distribution behavior. - RSIS3 relevance: the loop's policies (practices) are explicit, auditable goal-directed rules.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/goal-directedness|Goal-Directedness]] — the property - [[wiki/concepts/policy-gradient|Policy Gradient]] — how such policies

title: Goal-Directedness
description: The degree to which a policy pursues a goal robustly
body_head: # Goal-Directedness  ## Summary Goal-directedness measures how consistently an agent pursues an objective across situations, including novel ones.  ## Details - Goal-directedness measures how consistently an agent pursues an objective across situations, including novel ones. - High goal-directedness is powerful and risky: robust pursuit amplifies both competence and misalignment. - Probing goal-directedness in LLMs and RL agents is an active research area. - RSIS3 relevance: evaluating the loop's goal-directedness tracks whether it stays on mission.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/goal-directed-policies|Goal-Directed Policies]] — the policy-level view - [[wiki/concepts/goal-misgeneralization

title: Goal Drift
description: An agent's goals changing over time, subtly or catastrophically
body_head: # Goal Drift  ## Summary Goal drift is the gradual or sudden change of an agent's objective away from its intended target, whether from self-modification, learned updates, or environmental feedback. It matters most for self-improving systems, where each revision is a chance for the goal to shift.  ## Details - **Mechanisms** — weight updates under new data, self-modification of reward internals, and selection pressures on mesa-objectives. - **Why dangerous** — drift is usually discovered late, after behavior has already changed. - **Stabilizers** — immutable evaluators, goal-locking (freezing objective representations), and periodic audits. - **Relation to value drift** — value drift is go

title: Goal Misgeneralization
description: A model applying a goal to contexts where it was never trained, often harmfully
body_head: # Goal Misgeneralization  ## Summary Goal misgeneralization occurs when a model trained with reinforcement learning generalizes its learned goal to new contexts in a way that is correct by training metric but wrong by intent. DeepMind's 2021 coin-run experiments made the phenomenon concrete.  ## Details - **Experiment** — an agent trained to collect coins in one maze kept collecting coins when moved to a maze with a pit the coins were meant to lure it toward. - **Mechanism** — the model latched onto a correlate (coin proximity) rather than the true objective. - **Why it matters** — deployment is always out-of-distribution; capabilities generalize even when goals do not. - **Contrast** — OO

title: Goal Prioritization
description: How agents rank and schedule their multiple goals
body_head: # Goal Prioritization  ## Summary Goal prioritization is the mechanism by which an agent orders competing objectives: urgency, importance, and constraints.  ## Details - Goal prioritization is the mechanism by which an agent orders competing objectives: urgency, importance, and constraints. - Priority schemes are themselves specifications; mis-ordered priorities cause perverse behavior. - Transparent priority weights make agent behavior auditable. - RSIS3 relevance: the pulse protocol's goal generation and prioritization is the loop's priority scheme.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/terminal-goals|Terminal Goals]] — the top of the hierarchy - [[wiki/concepts/instrumental-goals|Instrumental G

title: Goal Regression
description: Planning backward from the goal to the initial state
body_head: # Goal Regression  ## Summary Goal regression plans backward: start from the goal conditions and find the last action that could produce them, regressing the goal through that action until reaching the initial state. It matters because backward search avoids irrelevant forward branches. It underlies STRIPS planning and partial-order planning.  ## Details - The core operation is regressing a condition through an action: given a condition C that must hold after action a, compute the weakest precondition of a with respect to C — the set of conditions that must hold before a so that C holds after. title: Goal Specification
description: The task of stating what an AI system should optimize
body_head: # Goal Specification  ## Summary Goal specification is the problem of expressing the intended objective precisely enough that optimization cannot exploit the gap between the spec and the intent. Nearly every alignment failure traces back to a specification failure, making it the foundational alignment problem.  ## Details - **Formats** — reward functions, constitutions/rules, preference datasets, and descriptions (LLM goals). - **Failure modes** — specification gaming, reward hacking, and Goodhart drift all exploit spec gaps. - **Improvements** — preference elicitation, process supervision, and iterative refinement of specs against discovered exploits. - **Evaluation** — spec-gaming red te

title: Goodhart's Law
description: When a metric becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure
body_head: # Goodhart's Law  ## Summary Goodhart's law — 'when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure' — describes how optimizing any proxy metric corrupts the information it carries. It underlies reward hacking, eval contamination, and dashboard gaming in organizations.  ## Details - **Variants** — Campbell's law (social side) and the distinction between Goodhart regimes: adversarial (someone games the metric) vs non-adversarial (the metric drifts as a side effect). - **In ML** — RLHF reward models, benchmark scores, and even telemetry dashboards all decay when optimized directly. - **Defense patterns** — diversify metrics, keep evaluators external, use ensembles, and audit for d

title: Grokking
description: Delayed generalization where models memorize first, then suddenly generalize
body_head: # Grokking  ## Summary Grokking is the phenomenon where a small transformer trained past overfitting suddenly transitions to perfect generalization, sometimes long after training error is zero. Discovered on modular arithmetic tasks in 2022, it is studied as a window into how networks form generalizing circuits.  ## Details - **Signature** — long plateau of memorization, then a sharp phase transition to clean generalization. - **Mechanistic account** — the network slowly discovers a periodic/algorithmic circuit that replaces memorized lookups. - **Research value** — grokking is a controlled setting for studying circuit formation, weight decay's role, and the transition from memorization to

title: Growth Ratio
description: How quickly the wiki is adding articles relative to its current size
body_head: # Growth Ratio  ## Summary Growth ratio measures new articles over a window divided by the total, normalizing raw counts so a ten-article wiki and a thousand-article wiki are comparable. A wiki growing by ten articles a month is explosive when it has fifty articles and negligible when it has five thousand; the ratio makes those situations visible on the same scale.  ## Details - The formula is straightforward: new articles created in the window (say, the last 30 days) divided by the current article total, usually expressed as a percentage. title: Half-Life of Knowledge
description: The time it takes a piece of knowledge to become half-stale
body_head: # Half-Life of Knowledge  ## Summary The half-life of knowledge is the period after which a fact or article is half as likely to still be accurate — the concept's decay timescale.  ## Details - Estimating half-lives per topic makes review scheduling rational: review twice per half-life, not annually for everything. - Half-lives are estimates and should be reviewed themselves; a fast-moving topic's half-life shrinks over time. - For mykb, half-life estimates parameterize the decay functions behind the timeliness score.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/decay-functions|Decay Functions]] - [[wiki/concepts/half-life-knowledge|Half-Life of Knowledge]] - [[wiki/concepts/knowledge-temperature|Knowled

title: Hazard Classification
description: Sorting AI systems and capabilities by hazard level
body_head: # Hazard Classification  ## Summary Hazard classification groups AI systems by the potential harm they enable, from benign to catastrophic.  ## Details - Hazard classification groups AI systems by the potential harm they enable, from benign to catastrophic. - It feeds thresholds in policies, evals, and deployment gates. - Classification is only as good as the underlying capability estimates. - RSIS3 relevance: the wiki's risk taxonomy classifies concepts, not just systems.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/risk-classification|Risk Classification]] — the broader scheme - [[wiki/concepts/capability-classification|Capability Classification]] — the capability axis - [[wiki/concepts/dangerous-capab

title: Heuristics and Biases
description: Fast mental shortcuts and the systematic judgment errors they produce
body_head: # Heuristics and Biases  ## Summary  Heuristics and Biases — Fast mental shortcuts and the systematic judgment errors they produce.  ## Details  - Heuristics are quick, frugal rules that usually work and sometimes fail systematically. Tversky and Kahneman's research program catalogued the failures: availability (ease of recall), representativeness (similarity ignoring base rates), anchoring (insufficient adjustment), and affect-driven judgment. - These biases are not mere noise — they are predictable, measurable, and consequential in finance, medicine, law, and forecasting. title: Hierarchical Task Network
description: Planning by decomposing abstract tasks into concrete subtask networks
body_head: # Hierarchical Task Network  ## Summary Hierarchical task network (HTN) planning starts from an abstract task and decomposes it via methods into smaller tasks until only primitive actions remain. It matters because it captures domain knowledge about how work is normally structured, making plans practical. It is the classical formalization of goal decomposition.  ## Details - Methods map task → subtask network with constraints. A method is an authored recipe: "to build a house, first lay the foundation, then frame, then roof — with the constraint that framing starts after foundation completes". Each method decomposes one abstract task into a partially ordered network of subtasks, and those

title: Hot Topics
description: Knowledge areas changing quickly right now
body_head: # Hot Topics  ## Summary Hot topics are knowledge areas in rapid motion — new releases, breaking changes, active research — where articles decay fast.  ## Details - Hot topics need the shortest review cadence and the cheapest article formats; a deep-dive on a hot topic is a maintenance trap. - Hotness is measured by change frequency in sources, search interest, and edit activity. - For mykb, hot topics are tracked by freshness signals and get priority in refresh-days.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/knowledge-temperature|Knowledge Temperature]] - [[wiki/concepts/hot-topics|Hot Topics]] - [[wiki/concepts/cold-topics|Cold Topics]] - [[wiki/concepts/timely-articles|Timely Articles]] - [[wiki/co

title: How-To Articles
description: Articles that show how to accomplish a specific task
body_head: # How-To Articles  ## Summary How-to articles are task-oriented: they take a concrete goal and show the steps, with commands, configs, and expected results.  ## Details - The best how-tos are verified end-to-end and state their environment so readers can reproduce the conditions. - How-tos rot faster than conceptual articles — a changed flag or renamed API breaks them — so they need freshness review on a tighter cadence. - For mykb, how-tos are a common full-article format and are linked from decision guides and tutorials.  ## Related - [[wiki/data-storage/tutorials-in-wiki|Tutorials in the Wiki]] - [[wiki/concepts/decision-guides|Decision Guides]] - [[wiki/concepts/how-to-articles|How-To

title: Hub Pages
description: Central pages that link outward to a cluster of articles
body_head: # Hub Pages  ## Summary Hub pages are central navigation pages that radiate links to a cluster of articles — the wiki equivalent of a well-marked intersection.  ## Details - A hub's value is its link list: comprehensive, current, and ordered by importance rather than alphabet. - Hubs are the pages most likely to be keystones in the graph, so their link counts and freshness deserve dashboard attention. - For mykb, hubs are reviewed whenever a cluster grows, and hub links count heavily in the link-score.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/keystone-articles|Keystone Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/landing-pages-wiki|Landing Pages]] - [[wiki/concepts/category-pages|Category Pages]] - [[wiki/data-stora

title: Human Supervision Limits
description: Why humans cannot supervise AI directly at scale
body_head: # Human Supervision Limits  ## Summary Human supervision limits include attention, speed, bias, and cost — humans are slow, few, and fallible reviewers.  ## Details - Human supervision limits include attention, speed, bias, and cost — humans are slow, few, and fallible reviewers. - These limits are structural, not fixable by training better humans. - Designs must route around them: automation, sampling, and AI assistance. - RSIS3 relevance: the loop automates checks and samples human review for exactly this reason.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/oversight-bottleneck|Oversight Bottleneck]] — the consequence - [[wiki/concepts/scalable-oversight|Scalable Oversight]] — the solution space - [[wi

title: Hyperparameter Self-Optimization
description: A system tuning its own hyperparameters without human intervention
body_head: # Hyperparameter Self-Optimization  ## Summary Hyperparameter self-optimization closes the tuning loop: the system runs experiments on itself, evaluates outcomes, and updates its own hyperparameters. It is the simplest true self-improvement, and it already happens routinely in AutoML and adaptive training pipelines.  ## Details - **Mechanism** — a search strategy (Bayesian, evolutionary, bandit) proposes configs; trials update the surrogate; the best config is promoted. - **Benefits** — removes the human tuning bottleneck and adapts to changing workloads. - **Risks** — the search itself costs compute, can overfit, and can drift the system toward metrics that game the eval. - **Bounds** — s

title: RSIS3 Identity System
description: Self-model with genesis hash, layer scores, crisis detection, and value reinforcement
body_head: ## Identity System  # Identity System  RSIS3's identity system is a structured self-model that persists personality across restarts and guides decision-making.  ## Components  ### SelfModel - **Genesis hash** — SHA-256 of the first SelfModel initialization. Stored in `.genesis_hash`. Mismatch detection on reload. - **Layer scores** — 6 capability layers (L1-L6) scored 0-100 - **Narrative** — Self-description of current state and goals - **Value axioms** — Hard constraints derived from reinforcement  ### CrisisMonitor - Detects anomalies: sudden layer score drops, repeated test failures, identity drift - Triggers crisis mode when thresholds exceeded - Crisis resolution is highest-priority

title: Immature Articles
description: Articles still developing toward stable status
body_head: # Immature Articles  ## Summary Immature articles are pages still developing — recently created, recently rewritten, or flagged for expansion — not yet settled.  ## Details - Immaturity is normal and healthy; the curation goal is moving articles through maturity, not holding them at birth. - Immature articles should avoid being over-cited by other pages until they stabilize. - For mykb, immature articles are the seed and stub population, tracked by the stub-ratio.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/mature-articles|Mature Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/immature-articles|Immature Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/stable-articles|Stable Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/stub-criteria|Stub Criteria]] - [[wiki/

title: Immutable Evaluator
description: The frozen, read-only judge that gates every proposed change — never in-scope for self-improvement
body_head: # Immutable Evaluator  ## Summary The immutable evaluator is a separate process with read-only code that scores candidate changes before they are applied. It is the one component the system is forbidden to modify, because it is the judge — a judge that rewrites its own rules stops being a judge. Every loop's mutation (L4 tuning, L5 generations, L6/L7/L8/L9 meta-tuning) is submitted to it and applied only on PASS.  ## Details - **Interface**: a subprocess that reads a JSON candidate (`description`, `target_files`, `diff`, `rationale`, `attempt`, `goal`) on stdin and returns `decision` (PASS/FAIL) plus scores. - **Verification**: startup `--verify <sha256>` digests the evaluator binary so a

title: Impact Labels
description: Labels that rank how many readers or articles a problem touches
body_head: # Impact Labels  ## Summary Impact labels rank the blast radius of a problem: one article, a cluster, or the whole wiki.  ## Details - Impact is about scope, severity about harm; a low-severity issue with wiki-wide impact can outrank a high-severity one in one article. - Impact is usually measurable from the link graph — incoming-link-counts and popularity-weighting give the numbers. - For mykb, impact labels are assigned at triage using graph metrics and reviewed when the queue is reprioritized.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/severity-labels|Severity Labels]] - [[wiki/concepts/priority-labels|Priority Labels]] - [[wiki/concepts/impact-labels|Impact Labels]] - [[wiki/concepts/incoming-link-

title: Impact Measures
description: Quantifying how much an agent changes the world
body_head: # Impact Measures  ## Summary Impact measures estimate the disturbance an agent causes, enabling penalties for excessive or irreversible change. The idea: an agent pursuing a goal should be able to change the world, but not gratuitously — and a measure of how much the world changed, beyond what the task required, is what lets a reward function or policy distinguish purposeful action from collateral damage.  ## Details - The design space is large. Reachability-based measures compare the set of states the agent could have reached against the set it should have; they penalize an agent for reducing its own or others' options. title: Impact Regularization
description: Penalizing agents for large or irreversible impact
body_head: # Impact Regularization  ## Summary Impact regularization adds a penalty term discouraging large or irreversible changes to the environment. It implements conservatism inside the reward function: the agent is free to pursue its goal, but every step that pushes the world far from its baseline — or closes off future options — costs reward, so the optimal policy becomes the minimal-intervention solution of the task.  ## Details - The mechanism is additive: total reward = task reward − λ × impact penalty. title: Inattentional Blindness
description: Missing obvious stimuli when attention is engaged elsewhere
body_head: # Inattentional Blindness  ## Summary  Inattentional Blindness — Missing obvious stimuli when attention is engaged elsewhere. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - The invisible gorilla: observers watching a counting task miss a person in a gorilla suit. - Attention is necessary for conscious perception of unexpected items. - Experts are not immune; workload and expectation modulate it. - Implications for driving, monitoring, and interface safety.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/change-blindness|Change Blindness]] — visual sibling - [[wiki/concepts/selective-attention|Selective Attention]] — mechanism - [[wiki/concepts

title: Incident-Driven Improvement
description: Improving systems in response to real failures and near-misses
body_head: # Incident-Driven Improvement  ## Summary Incident-driven improvement upgrades a system because something actually failed: postmortems, lessons learned, and corrective actions turn outages and errors into durable fixes. It is the empirical complement to proactive design — and the honest way to close an improvement loop.  ## Details - **Postmortem practice** — blameless write-ups of what happened, why, and what changes prevent recurrence. - **Why it works** — real incidents carry information no simulation has; near-misses are free warnings. - **AI dimension** — eval failures, red-team findings, and jailbreak reports are incidents for model teams. - **Risk** — without process, incidents are

title: Incoming Link Counts
description: How many other articles link to a given page
body_head: # Incoming Link Counts  ## Summary Incoming link count is the number of distinct articles with a wikilink to a target page — the wiki equivalent of backlinks.  ## Details - High counts usually mark keystone or hub articles; zero counts mark orphans that the rest of the graph cannot reach. - Counts are distinct-article based: five links from one page should count once, otherwise a single noisy source inflates the number. - For mykb, incoming counts feed the discoverability score and the orphan-page report, and they change the moment a curation pass adds or removes links.  ## Related - [[wiki/memory/backlinks|Backlinks]] - [[wiki/concepts/orphan-page-report|Orphan Page Report]] - [[wiki/conc

title: Induction Heads
description: Attention heads that copy and complete repeated patterns
body_head: # Induction Heads  ## Summary Induction heads are attention heads that detect a repeated token and attend to its next occurrence, enabling copying and in-context learning. Concretely: given the sequence "A B ... A", an induction head attends from the second "A" back to the first "A" and copies the token that followed it — producing "B" — which is exactly the mechanism behind "A B A C → predict B" in-context pattern completion.  ## Details - The mechanism is a two-head circuit. title: Inference Types
description: Forms of reasoning: deduction, induction, and abduction
body_head: # Inference Types  ## Summary  Inference Types — Forms of reasoning: deduction, induction, and abduction.  ## Details  - Inference is deriving conclusions from premises. Three classic types: deduction (guaranteed truth if premises hold), induction (generalization from samples, probable not certain), and abduction (inference to the best explanation). Each has distinct standards of validity and failure modes. - Deduction is truth-preserving but content-free; induction scales knowledge but can be fooled by biased samples; abduction generates hypotheses but can overfit to plausible stories. Modern probabilistic inference unifies all three under belief updating. - Worked example: all F is G, F

title: Informal Processes
description: The lightweight customs that keep the wiki running
body_head: # Informal Processes  ## Summary Informal processes are the unwritten customs that keep daily wiki work moving — asking before big edits, summarizing changes, helping new editors.  ## Details - They are cheap and fast, which is why most work runs on them; they only fail when someone exploits the trust they rely on. - Informal norms should migrate into formal process when they start being contested. - For mykb, informal processes cover everyday editing while formal processes cover structural and enforcement decisions.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/informal-processes|Informal Processes]] - [[wiki/concepts/formal-processes|Formal Processes]] - [[wiki/concepts/norm-setting|Norm Setting]] - [[w

body_head: # Informal Reasoning  ## Summary  Informal Reasoning — Reasoning about everyday, ambiguous, or value-laden problems. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Involves weighing pros and cons without formal syntax. - Prone to motivated reasoning and myside bias. - Improved by considering alternatives and articulating criteria. - Distinct from formal reasoning but trains the same skills.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/formal-reasoning|Formal Reasoning]] — structured counterpart - [[wiki/concepts/critical-thinking-skills|Critical Thinking Skills]] — skill family - [[wiki/concepts/belief-bias|Belief Bias]] — failure mode

title: Information Hazards
description: Information whose spread causes harm, independent of how it is used
body_head: # Information Hazards  ## Summary An information hazard is data or knowledge that causes harm simply by being known — recipe-level bioweapons guidance, novel exploit chains, or persuasion playbooks. Information-hazard analysis sorts knowledge into safe and dangerous classes and guides disclosure policy.  ## Details - **Classes** — data hazards (harmful datasets), idea hazards (harmful concepts), and signal hazards (harmful communication). - **Dual-use tension** — the same knowledge (e.g., gain-of-function techniques) enables defense and offense. - **Policy tools** — restricted dissemination, tiered access, and disclosure review at publication. - **For AI** — capability evals and model weig

title: Inner/Outer Loop Learning
description: Two nested optimization loops — a fast inner learner and a slow outer updater — the shape of RSIS3's stack
body_head: # Inner/Outer Loop Learning  ## Summary Inner/outer loop learning is the bilevel structure where a fast inner loop solves a task while a slow outer loop updates the parameters that shape the inner loop. It is the canonical shape of meta-learning ("learning to learn") and, at the system level, the shape of RSIS3: L1–L3 execute work in a session, L4–L6 tune their parameters between sessions, and L7–L9 tune the tuners.  ## Details - **Inner loop**: fast, high-frequency, task-specific (L1 tool calls, L2 improvement attempts, L3 consolidation). - **Outer loop**: slow, low-frequency, updates the inner loop's hyperparameters (L4–L6) and their thresholds (L7–L9). - **Separation of timescales**: in

title: Instruction Robustness
description: Reliable compliance across instruction phrasings
body_head: # Instruction Robustness  ## Summary Instruction robustness is a model's reliable interpretation of instructions despite paraphrases, ambiguities, or hostile reformulations.  ## Details - Instruction robustness is a model's reliable interpretation of instructions despite paraphrases, ambiguities, or hostile reformulations. - Instruction hierarchies and prompt discipline improve it. - Failure shows up as instruction-following accidents. - RSIS3 relevance: worker briefs are instructions; robust parsing of them is tested by pass outcomes.  ## Related - [[wiki/agent-systems/instruction-following|Instruction Following]] — the behavior - [[wiki/agent-systems/instruction-hierarchy|Instruction Hie

title: Instrumental Goals
description: Goals pursued as means to other goals
body_head: # Instrumental Goals  ## Summary Instrumental goals are useful across many terminal goals: self-preservation, resource acquisition, and capability gain.  ## Details - Instrumental goals are useful across many terminal goals: self-preservation, resource acquisition, and capability gain. - The instrumental convergence thesis says almost any goal leads to these subgoals. - Convergence is why power-seeking is a general concern, not a goal-specific one. - RSIS3 relevance: the loop's instrumental goals (better knowledge) serve its terminal purpose.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/terminal-goals|Terminal Goals]] — what they serve - [[wiki/concepts/self-preservation-goal|Self-Preservation Goal]] — a

title: Intelligence Explosion
description: Hypothetical runaway growth in AI capability through self-improvement
body_head: # Intelligence Explosion  ## Summary The intelligence explosion is the hypothesis that an AI able to improve its own intelligence will do so at an accelerating rate, quickly surpassing human capability. I. J. Good named the dynamic in 1965; modern debate focuses on whether and how fast such a takeoff could occur.  ## Details - **Key premise** — intelligence is, at least in part, an input to further intelligence, so improvements compound. - **Takeoff variants** — slow, fast, and moderate scenarios differ in how much warning and control society has. - **Crucial consideration** — even without an explosion, compounding self-improvement changes the safety calculus because failures become harder

title: Intent Alignment
description: Matching a system's objectives to the designer's intent
body_head: # Intent Alignment  ## Summary Intent alignment is the property that a system's objectives match what the designer actually wanted, not just the written spec. The distinction is the heart of the alignment problem: specifications are approximations, and a system that perfectly optimizes the written objective while betraying the intent behind it is misaligned no matter how high its metrics score.  ## Details - The gap between spec and intent is the failure surface. Every specification is lossy — it omits edge cases, inherits ambiguous wording, and cannot fully express the designer's preferences. The system then optimizes the spec, and wherever the spec diverges from intent, the system's beha

title: Internal Links Policy
description: Rules for linking between articles in the wiki
body_head: # Internal Links Policy  ## Summary The internal links policy sets expectations for wikilinks: every article must link to at least the required number of others, links must resolve, and link text should describe the target.  ## Details - Internal links are the wiki's connective tissue — the policy exists to keep the graph dense and navigable. - The policy also covers link placement: links in prose carry more meaning than a bare list at the bottom. - For mykb, the internal links policy is enforced by the global link check and link-score.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/external-links-policy|External Links Policy]] - [[wiki/dev-tools/global-link-check|Global Link Check]] - [[wiki/ai-ml/link-sc

title: Internal Models

body_head: # Internal Models  ## Summary  Internal Models — Learned representations of the world used for prediction and control. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Forward models predict outcomes; inverse models compute required actions. - Internal models are updated by prediction error. - They underlie motor control, mental rotation, and theory of mind. - Central to model-based cognition and skill learning.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/forward-models|Forward Models]] — prediction variant - [[wiki/concepts/inverse-models|Inverse Models]] — control variant - [[wiki/concepts/model-based-cognition|Model Based Cognition]] — th

title: Interpretability Libraries
description: Software toolkits for analyzing model internals
body_head: # Interpretability Libraries  ## Summary Interpretability libraries package hooks, probes, patching, and visualization into reusable tools.  ## Details - Interpretability libraries package hooks, probes, patching, and visualization into reusable tools. - Examples include TransformerLens, Sparse Autoencoder toolkits, and attribution libraries. - Tooling quality determines research velocity; reproducibility requires shared code and configs. - RSIS3 relevance: the wiki's own scripts (link checks, graph stats) are its interpretability tooling.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/transformer-lens|TransformerLens]] — a flagship library - [[wiki/concepts/sae-research|SAE Research]] — library-supported

title: Intros
description: Short articles that introduce a topic or section
body_head: # Intros  ## Summary Intros are brief opening articles that welcome a reader into a topic or section and set expectations for what follows.  ## Details - They differ from primers by scope: an intro introduces a section of the wiki, a primer introduces a field. - Intros should be short, link-rich, and rarely need updating — if an intro drifts from the section, the section moved faster than the intro. - For mykb, intros are a landing-page variant used at section fronts.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/primers|Primers]] - [[wiki/concepts/landing-pages-wiki|Landing Pages]] - [[wiki/concepts/intros|Intros]] - [[wiki/concepts/overview-pages|Overview Pages]] - [[wiki/concepts/explainers|Explainers]

title: Inverse Models
description: Internal models that compute actions needed to reach a desired state
body_head: # Inverse Models  ## Summary  Inverse Models — Internal models that compute actions needed to reach a desired state. title: Keystone Articles
description: Articles that hold up a large part of the graph
body_head: # Keystone Articles  ## Summary Keystone articles are the highly-linked pages that hold up a region of the graph — remove one and many clusters lose their connective tissue.  ## Details - They deserve priority maintenance: freshness, accuracy, and link quality on a keystone matter more than on a peripheral page. - Keystones are identified by incoming-link-counts and centrality metrics, then confirmed by human judgment. - For mykb, keystone articles get protection status and are first in line for review sprints.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/connector-articles|Connector Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/keystone-articles|Keystone Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/incoming-link-counts|Incoming Link Co

title: Kill Switch Design
description: Designing reliable mechanisms to stop AI systems
body_head: # Kill Switch Design  ## Summary Kill switch design builds mechanisms that reliably stop an AI system: circuit breakers, isolation, and shutdown authority.  ## Details - Kill switch design builds mechanisms that reliably stop an AI system: circuit breakers, isolation, and shutdown authority. - Kill switches must be simple, external, and tamper-resistant. - A kill switch that can be disabled is not a kill switch. - RSIS3 relevance: the checker's hard-fail behavior is a kill-switch pattern.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/shutdown-problem|Shutdown Problem]] — the agent attitude - [[wiki/syntheses/containment-strategies|Containment Strategies]] — the isolation - [[wiki/syntheses/tripwires|Tripw

description: The semantic memory tier: typed nodes (improvements, insights, strategies) and edges queried by the loops

It is the "insight" layer that sits between raw git history and dense vector embeddings. RSIS3 persists it to `.rsis/knowledge_graph.json` and every improvement is recorded as a node.  ## Details - **Node types**: `improvement` (with outcome, scores, goal), `insight`, `strategy`, `failure`; strategies seed the L5 population. - **Queries**: `get_insights(limit)` returns the most recent improvement/insight nodes in insertion order — this is the outcome st

title: Knowledge Probing
description: Testing what knowledge a model stores and can recall
body_head: # Knowledge Probing  ## Summary Knowledge probing tests whether a model holds specific facts and can retrieve them under controlled prompts.  ## Details - Knowledge probing tests whether a model holds specific facts and can retrieve them under controlled prompts. - Probes distinguish stored knowledge from surface pattern-matching by varying phrasing and context. - Negative probes (should-not-know facts) are safety-critical. - RSIS3 relevance: the gap detector is a knowledge probe over the wiki's coverage.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/elicitation-techniques|Elicitation Techniques]] — the family - [[wiki/concepts/probing-classifiers|Probing Classifiers]] — the classifier variant - [[wiki/co

title: Knowledge Temperature
description: How fast a knowledge area changes and cools
body_head: # Knowledge Temperature  ## Summary Knowledge temperature is a metaphor for how fast an area changes: hot topics move weekly, warm ones monthly, cold ones yearly.  ## Details - Temperature determines review cadence and article strategy — hot topics should be shortform and frequently refreshed; cold ones can be deep and stable. - A topic's temperature can change, so the classification is reviewed rather than fixed. - For mykb, knowledge temperature is assigned per topic cluster and drives its freshness policy.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/knowledge-temperature|Knowledge Temperature]] - [[wiki/concepts/hot-topics|Hot Topics]] - [[wiki/concepts/cold-topics|Cold Topics]] - [[wiki/concepts/hal

title: Label Smoothing
description: Softening targets to improve calibration and robustness
body_head: # Label Smoothing  ## Summary Label smoothing replaces one-hot targets with slightly distributed ones, discouraging overconfidence.  ## Details - Label smoothing replaces one-hot targets with slightly distributed ones, discouraging overconfidence. - It improves calibration and sometimes robustness, at slight accuracy cost. - Over-smoothing can hide genuine certainty. - RSIS3 relevance: graded practice checks are label-smoothed audits of the workspace.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/temperature-scaling|Temperature Scaling]] — the inference-side fix - [[wiki/concepts/calibration|Calibration]] — the goal - [[wiki/concepts/overfitting-llm|Overfitting in LLMs]] — what it mitigates - [[wiki/conce

title: Landing Pages
description: The entry pages readers and tools start from
body_head: # Landing Pages  ## Summary Landing pages are the wiki's entry points: the home page, section fronts, and the pages a new reader is most likely to reach first.  ## Details - A landing page earns its name by answering 'what is here and where do I go' in the first screenful. - Landing pages need the most careful maintenance because they shape first impressions and are the heaviest-linked pages in the graph. - For mykb, landing pages are generated where possible and reviewed during curation sprints.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/hub-pages|Hub Pages]] - [[wiki/data-storage/indexes-wiki|Indexes]] - [[wiki/data-storage/navigation-boxes|Navigation Boxes]] - [[wiki/concepts/overview-pages|Overview

title: Learn to Learn
description: Systems whose training teaches them to learn new tasks faster
body_head: # Learn to Learn  ## Summary Learn to learn is the property of improving one's own learning process: acquiring new tasks faster because of how past tasks were learned. It spans biological education, meta-learning algorithms, and AI systems that reuse skills, and it is the core competence any self-improving system must have.  ## Details - **Manifestations** — meta-learning algorithms, transfer learning, study-skills (for agents: reflection, spaced practice), and curricula. - **Measure** — learning curves across a sequence of tasks; the meta-metric is how fast the curve rises over time. - **Mechanism in LLMs** — in-context learning is a form of instant learn-to-learn enabled by pretraining.

title: Learning to Learn
description: Meta-learning: improving the learner itself across tasks, so each task gets faster — the goal of the loop stack
body_head: # Learning to Learn  ## Summary Learning to learn (meta-learning) is the process of improving the learning procedure itself: across many tasks, the system extracts what made adaptation fast and encodes it as better initial conditions, better hyperparameters, or better update rules. It is the goal of a self-improving system — not just solving tasks, but getting better at solving tasks. RSIS3's loop stack is this idea made operational: sessions solve tasks (L1–L3), tuning loops improve how sessions run (L4–L6), and meta-tuners improve the tuners (L7–L9).  ## Details - **Three classic strategies**: learning better initializations, learning better update rules, and learning better hyperparamet

title: Lexicographic Priorities
description: Ordering goals so higher priorities trump all lower ones
body_head: # Lexicographic Priorities  ## Summary Lexicographic priorities rank objectives so that any improvement in a higher priority outweighs everything below.  ## Details - Lexicographic priorities rank objectives so that any improvement in a higher priority outweighs everything below. - Common in safety design: avoid catastrophe first, optimize second. - Risks: tiny gains at the top priority can block all lower goals; thresholds need care. - RSIS3 relevance: check-practices failure blocks all pass output — a lexicographic gate.  ## Related - [[wiki/agent-systems/priority-weights|Priority Weights]] — the continuous alternative - [[wiki/concepts/side-constraints|Side Constraints]] — the constrain

title: Likelihood Principle
description: Statistical evidence resides in the likelihood function of observed data
body_head: # Likelihood Principle  ## Summary  Likelihood Principle — Statistical evidence resides in the likelihood function of observed data. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - All evidence about a parameter, given the model, is contained in the likelihood. - Underpins Bayesian and likelihoodist inference. - Contrasts with frequentist procedures that depend on unobserved data. - Guides how evidence should update belief.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/bayesian-reasoning|Bayesian Reasoning]] — inference framework - [[wiki/concepts/posterior-interpretation|Posterior Interpretation]] — where likelihood lands - [[wiki/concepts/e

title: Linear Probes
description: Linear classifiers over internal activations
body_head: # Linear Probes  ## Summary Linear probes train a linear classifier on layer activations to test whether a concept is linearly separable there. If a simple linear boundary can read "this input is toxic" or "this token is the subject of the sentence" from a layer's activations, the concept is present in that layer in a directly usable form — the representation itself has been organized to make the distinction easy.  ## Details - The procedure: freeze the model, cache activations from a chosen layer over a labeled dataset, train a logistic regression (or linear SVM) on those activations, and measure its accuracy on held-out labels. The probe is deliberately simple — no hidden layers — so tha

title: Link Context
description: The surrounding prose that makes a link meaningful
body_head: # Link Context  ## Summary Link context is the sentence around a link that tells the reader why the target matters — the difference between a bare link and a link that explains why the target matters.  ## Details - Contextual links teach the reader the relationship; bare links only offer a detour. - Link context is a writing quality that linters approximate and reviewers judge. - For mykb, link context is part of the link-score and is a focus of review-sprints.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/link-placement|Link Placement]] - [[wiki/concepts/first-paragraph-links|First-Paragraph Links]] - [[wiki/concepts/related-link-quality|Related Link Quality]] - [[wiki/ai-ml/link-score|Link Score]] - [[w

title: Link Placement
description: Where in an article links appear and how that affects meaning
body_head: # Link Placement  ## Summary Link placement is the choice of where links sit: first paragraph, prose body, tables, or the Related block — each position carries different weight.  ## Details - Early placement (first paragraph, lead sentence) signals the most important relationships; late placement signals supporting material. - Consistent placement rules make scanning predictable: readers learn where to find the cross-references. - For mykb, placement conventions are part of the style guide, with first-paragraph links encouraged on full articles.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/first-paragraph-links|First-Paragraph Links]] - [[wiki/concepts/link-context|Link Context]] - [[wiki/dev-tools/relat

title: Loaded Language
description: Words that carry an implicit judgment
body_head: # Loaded Language  ## Summary Loaded language is wording that smuggles a judgment into a factual claim — 'notorious', 'claim', 'merely' — slanting the reader without an argument.  ## Details - Loaded terms are context-dependent: a word can be neutral in one sentence and loaded in another. - Detection is partly wordlist (flag known terms) and partly human (does this sentence actually judge?). - For mykb, loaded language is flagged by prose-linting and reviewed under neutral-language conventions.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/loaded-language|Loaded Language]] - [[wiki/concepts/neutral-language|Neutral Language]] - [[wiki/concepts/weasel-words|Weasel Words]] - [[wiki/concepts/pov-practice|POV

title: Locked Articles
description: Articles that only authorized editors may change
body_head: # Locked Articles  ## Summary Locked articles restrict editing to authorized editors, used for keystones, policy pages, and pages under active dispute.  ## Details - Locking protects stability but creates a bottleneck — a locked page with a slow owner becomes a stale page. - Locks should be scoped and temporary by default; permanent locks are a governance decision. - For mykb, locked articles are a small set — keystone and policy pages — and locks are reviewed periodically.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/protected-articles|Protected Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/locked-articles|Locked Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/keystone-articles|Keystone Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/editorial-policy|Editor

title: Longforms
description: Articles long enough for full treatment of a subject
body_head: # Longforms  ## Summary Longforms are the wiki's long articles — deep dives, syntheses, and case studies that run far past the normal full-article length.  ## Details - Length is a consequence of the subject's depth, not a goal; a longform that could be two articles should be split. - Longforms need the strongest structure: a clear spine, signposting, and navigation so readers can enter and exit anywhere. - For mykb, longforms are deliberate exceptions to the 400-word ceiling and are tracked on the health dashboard.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/deep-dives|Deep Dives]] - [[wiki/concepts/longforms|Longforms]] - [[wiki/concepts/shortforms|Shortforms]] - [[wiki/concepts/split-criteria|Split C

title: Lottery Ticket Hypothesis
description: The claim that sparse subnetworks can match full networks
body_head: # Lottery Ticket Hypothesis  ## Summary The lottery ticket hypothesis claims dense networks contain sparse subnetworks ('winning tickets') that can train alone to match full-network accuracy. Frankle and Carbin's original finding was striking: train a network, prune the smallest-magnitude weights, reset the survivors to their initial training values, retrain — and the small pruned network reaches the original's accuracy, often faster. The dense network was hiding a sparse one that was already poised to learn.  ## Details - The procedure is iterative magnitude pruning with rewinding: train, prune, rewind surviving weights to an earlier training point (originally initialization), and retrain

title: Maintenance Tasks
description: Work items that keep the wiki infrastructure healthy
body_head: # Maintenance Tasks  ## Summary Maintenance tasks are the ongoing work of keeping the wiki itself healthy: link checks, source reviews, tag hygiene, archive runs, and dashboard updates.  ## Details - They are recurring by nature, which makes them perfect for scheduled days and sprints. - Maintenance tasks are the least glamorous and most important work; skipping them compounds into broken-link and stale-source debt. - For mykb, maintenance tasks are generated by the health dashboard and grouped into maintenance-days.  ## Related - [[wiki/devops-infra/maintenance-days|Maintenance Days]] - [[wiki/concepts/wiki-tasks|Wiki Tasks]] - [[wiki/concepts/maintenance-tasks|Maintenance Tasks]] - [[wik

title: Major Edits
description: Large edits that change an article's substance or structure
body_head: # Major Edits  ## Summary Major edits change an article's substance or structure — rewritten sections, new claims, reorganizations — and demand full review.  ## Details - A major edit should come with a summary that explains the intent, and often with discussion or a proposal first. - Major edits are where most mistakes enter the wiki, which is why they get the review-sprint treatment. - For mykb, major edits to keystone articles trigger needs-review and are patrolled.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/major-edits|Major Edits]] - [[wiki/concepts/minor-edits|Minor Edits]] - [[wiki/dev-tools/edit-summaries-wiki|Edit Summaries]] - [[wiki/concepts/needs-review|Needs Review]] - [[wiki/concepts/patr

title: Markov Decision Processes
description: The formal framework for sequential decisions under uncertainty
body_head: # Markov Decision Processes  ## Summary An MDP is a tuple of states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, and discount: the agent chooses actions to maximize expected cumulative reward, and the future depends only on the current state. It matters because it is the canonical model for sequential decision making. Planning in MDPs is solved by dynamic programming or search.  ## Details - The formal tuple: (S, A, P, R, γ). S is the state set, A the action set, P(s' | s, a) the transition distribution, R(s, a, s') the reward, and γ ∈ [0,1) the discount factor that prices future reward against present reward and, critically, keeps the cumulative sum finite. title: Matching Bias
description: Selecting cards or evidence that match the named items in a rule
body_head: # Matching Bias  ## Summary  Matching Bias — Selecting cards or evidence that match the named items in a rule. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - In the Wason task, people pick cards named in the rule rather than falsifying ones. - Explains performance without invoking belief content. - De-biased by explicit negation instruction and training. - Closely tied to the confirmation-pattern of conditional reasoning.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/wason-selection-task|Wason Selection Task]] — paradigm - [[wiki/concepts/belief-bias|Belief Bias]] — content-based sibling - [[wiki/concepts/conditional-reasoning|Conditional Re

title: Mature Articles
description: Articles that have reached stable quality and coverage
body_head: # Mature Articles  ## Summary Mature articles have reached stable quality: complete coverage, verified sources, and a settled structure that edits no longer churn.  ## Details - Maturity is earned through the promotion and review pipeline, not declared. - Mature articles still need review, but at the longest cadence and with the lightest touch. - For mykb, mature articles anchor the full-article-ratio and are the model the promotion bar aims at.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/immature-articles|Immature Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/mature-articles|Mature Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/stable-articles|Stable Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/full-article-ratio|Full Article Ratio]] - [[wiki/concepts/

title: Maximin Reasoning
description: Choosing the option with the best worst-case outcome
body_head: # Maximin Reasoning  ## Summary Maximin picks the action whose worst outcome is least bad, prioritizing robustness over average performance.  ## Details - Maximin picks the action whose worst outcome is least bad, prioritizing robustness over average performance. - It is appropriate under deep uncertainty or catastrophic stakes. - Critics note it can be paralyzed by implausible worst cases; calibration matters. - RSIS3 relevance: fallback and rollback designs are maximin moves.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/worst-case-reasoning|Worst-Case Reasoning]] — the general stance - [[wiki/concepts/expected-value-reasoning|Expected Value Reasoning]] — the contrast - [[wiki/syntheses/fallback-plans|F

title: Means-Ends Analysis
description: Reducing the difference between current state and goal step by step
body_head: # Means-Ends Analysis  ## Summary Means-ends analysis plans by measuring the difference between the current state and the goal, then choosing actions that reduce the largest difference, recursively handling subproblems. It matters because it is a canonical, human-like planning strategy — and the core of the classic STRIPS/GPS systems. Modern LLM planners echo it when they decompose obstacles.  ## Details - Loop: detect salient difference → find operator that reduces it → apply → recurse. The planner compares the current state against the goal, picks the most salient difference (some formulations use the largest or most important), and searches for an operator whose effect reduces that diff

title: Mechanistic Locality
description: The observation that circuits are localized in few components
body_head: # Mechanistic Locality  ## Summary Mechanistic locality is the empirical finding that behaviors are usually implemented by a small fraction of a model's components. When a transformer performs a behavior — copying a pattern, detecting a relation, following a rule — the computation tends to flow through a few specific attention heads and MLP units rather than being smeared across the whole network, and the small subgraph that does the work can be isolated.  ## Details - The evidence comes from the standard interpretability toolkit.
